news.title: Melania Cornered on Stealing Credit From Pope
news.text:
Melania Trump is considering a trip to war-torn Ukraine after triumphantly announcing on Friday that she had personally brokered a localized ceasefire in the country. 

After Melania and her husband, President Donald Trump, cast their votes in the midterm elections at a West Palm Beach, Florida, polling location on Saturday near their Mar-a-Lago home, the first lady was asked whether she planned to visit Ukraine.

“We will see,” she replied cryptically, before quickly turning around and leaving the venue. 

“It could happen,” the president added as he followed close behind his wife. 

Melania ignited a firestorm Friday after the White House credited her with single-handedly securing a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, in the city of Oleshky.

The ceasefire is intended to allow evacuations and the delivery of vital supplies to the city, whose residents have endured food shortages and disease after years of war. 

Despite the great fanfare Melania’s statement generated inside the administration, outside the White House she was quickly slammed and accused of trying to steal credit from Pope Leo. 

The cancer-stricken pontiff had called Russian President Vladimir Putin to request a ceasefire in Oleshky one week before Melania announced her own deal.

The pope made the call from his hospital bed, where he was recovering from surgery following a lung cancer diagnosis. 

Melania’s top adviser, Marc Beckman, appeared to brush aside the pope’s earlier intervention, insisting the achievement belonged to the first lady alone. 

“Yesterday she brokered—single-handedly brokered—a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine within the area of Oleshky,” Beckman told Fox & Friends Weekend on Saturday.

In fact, according to Beckman, it was Melania who inspired the pope to get involved in the cause—not the other way around. 

The president is also sticking by his wife’s account of how the negotiations went down, claiming to reporters that she is “doing better than the professionals right now.”

“It is great to have [the] pope’s support,” Melania added. 

The Daily Beast has reached out to the first lady’s office for comment.

Vatican officials, including Secretary of State Cardinal Pietro Parolin, have maintained that the ceasefire was indeed the pope’s initiative, contradicting the Trumps’ version of events.

Ukrainian official Davyd Arakhamia thanked both Melania and Pope Leo for their efforts in achieving the localized ceasefire, describing it as the culmination of a long process involving all sides.

Israel's army didn't respond to questions about the operation. On Friday, it said its forces had begun "conducting precise, targeted and thorough searches" in the area from where the gunmen operated.Death toll from church attack in Jordan rises to 9An ninth person died after gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in Jordan, state television reported. Saudi Arabia did not respond to a request for comment. The Associated Press couldn't independently verify the claims.At least two explosions were later heard near the international airport in Yemen's southern city of Aden, the seat of the internationally recognized government. The Houthi military spokesperson said a military camp and a naval base were targeted. The government's interior ministry said the Houthis attacked the coast guard headquarters at its complex with two ballistic missiles.The Saudi-led coalition earlier said it intercepted three ballistic missiles fired by the Houthis toward the Saudi capital, Riyadh, and Taif and Yanbu cities.The UAE closes beaches after oil spill from tankerThe United Arab Emirates closed beaches after an oil spill from a tanker. The spill impacted beaches of Umm Al Quwain, one of the seven emirates making up the federation, and cleanup efforts were underway, the Climate Change and Environment Ministry said.The ministry said the spill poses no health risks but did not provide details about its scale. We were holding talks, and they disrupted them." Anxiety has been growing in Iran and elsewhere that the U.S. or Israel will resume attacks before or just after Tuesday's elections in Israel or the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3.

news.title: Trump’s Midterm Test
news.text:
By Aakar Patel

Next week, on 3 November, America will have its midterm election. It is so called because it is held in the middle of a president’s four-year term. American parliamentarians, called Congressmen, face elections every two years. A lame duck president is the term used to describe a leader in his first two years in office, as Trump will be after 3 November. A lame duck is a leader who the party recognises is in riding into the sunset and therefore finds it difficult to enforce his agenda.

Donald Trump will be especially lame if his party, the Republicans, lose control of one or both houses of their parliament. He will not be able to get legislation he wants passed, will not be able to get judges appointed or get officials confirmed. Equally importantly the Opposition can go after him and his family by opening up investigations and then holding impeachment and other types of hearings.

The reason this election is interesting is that it will reveal something about human nature. The assumption of democratic systems is that individuals vote rationally and do not vote in tribal fashion – that they cast ballots in support of policies and not fantasies, particularly when the person produces negative outcomes when in office.

Opinion polls suggest that Trump is the most unpopular president in recent history. The majority of Americans, including those who voted for him into office, think he is doing a poor job. This is revealed through something called an approval rating, conducted regularly by several reputable polling organisations. A question is asked, such as: ‘Do you approve or disapprove of the way President Trump is doing his job?’ Respondents say yes, no or that they are unable to say. Trump’s approval rating is under 40%, meaning that a significant majority of Americans disapprove of his performance.

On his performance on the economy, which is asked as a separate question, the numbers are worse. This is not difficult to accept as true because the price of fuel has gone up and made things expensive since February and the war in Iran. Petrol in the US was Rs 75/litre before the war and is today Rs 107. Diesel has jumped from Rs 90 to Rs 160. Inflation is higher than the Federal Reserve (their version of the RBI) wants it and part of the reason is the tariff war that Trump began gratuitously on returning to power. The interest on home loans has gone up by a full percent.

Now, given that he has been in office since January last year and that his party controls both houses of Congress (and also controls the Supreme Court, whose judges are nominated by the president) there is nobody else to blame but Donald Trump if voters feel things haven’t turned out as they expected. Trump has endorsed these current candidates over their Republican opponents and therefore a vote for them is a vote for him and his policies.

And for this reason, the result of next week’s election will be interesting and give us some insight into how people vote. If most of Trump’s candidates carry the day despite the manifest harm he has wrought on their everyday lives it will be a vote for tribalism- meaning a vote for considerations in defiance of those that are material.

The other most interesting thing that these elections will show is how the unpopularity of Israel among Americans will convert to an end to unconditional support for it.

Many of the Democrats running in this cycle are staunchly anti-Israel, in keeping with the mood in America which has turned sharply against Zionism. In large part this is due to the brave campaign last year run by New York mayor Zohran Mamdani, who was the first major American politician to support Palestinians and still win.

The lobby group in America, called AIPAC, that had the ability to destroy anti-Israel candidates has since been discredited so thoroughly that it has stopped endorsing candidates.

Assuming the Democrats carry the day, will they be able to end the structural support that Israel has long enjoyed? We will see and one hopes that the answer is yes. Far too much damage has been done to humanity by Israelis and stopping or slowing the transfer of weaponry and diplomatic support to them would make the world better.

Another reason for hoping that Trump’s team loses is of course is that this mad war is affecting all of us and especially the one crore Indians in the Gulf and their families here. How insane all of it is can be judged by the fact that with oil at over $115 a barrel (it was at $60 before the war), there is talk in Washington and Tel Aviv about restarting bombing and further damaging Iran and the Gulf’s infrastructure.

A Republican party trounced next week will not as enthusiastically back the Iran war as it has.

The last thing to say here is that the two-year Congressional term is often criticised, rightly, because it means candidates are forever campaigning. But it is also true that the short cycle gives American voters a more frequent opportunity to correct the course of government when politicians do things that harm them. For their sake, and for the sake of all of us, one hopes that is what they do this time and not simply show up to vote for their ideology.

news.title: World News | Europe Swarmed by Wave of Protests as People March in France, Albania, Italy, Spain, Portugal
news.text:
Paris [France], October 25 (ANI): Europe is reeling under a fresh wave of protests as people march over the rising cost of living, pensions, housing, education, corruption and opposition to war. Groups across France, Albania, Italy, Spain and Portugal have held demonstrations in multiple cities, leading to clashes between protesters and police.

According to Euronews, authorities across several European capitals stepped up security measures following violence during earlier demonstrations, deploying large numbers of police personnel and, in some areas, soldiers.

Also Read | Dubai Gold Rate Today: 18K, 22K, 24K Gold Prices for October 24, 2026.

In France, nearly 1,000 people were arrested during Saturday's protests, with Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez saying the figure was likely to increase. The French government said 410,000 protesters had taken to the streets across the country, while organisers put the figure at nearly 800,000.

According to France 24, authorities announced that the demonstration in Paris had been completely dispersed along the Cours de Vincennes following clashes between protesters and law enforcement personnel.

Also Read | Oleshky Ceasefire: How Melania Trump's Back Channel With Vladimir Putin Helped Secure Ukraine Truce.

"A Gendarmerie helicopter has been deployed to support ground units and locate any remaining groups of rioters," the prefectural police said, adding that "more than 500 rioters" had been present towards the end of the demonstration. Police used water cannons and tear gas grenades after projectiles were thrown at them.

"As I speak to you, we are at nearly 1,000 arrests," Nunez said during a press briefing, adding, "I believe this figure will increase significantly."

He noted that 385 arrests had been made by the same time the previous Saturday, which had witnessed violence and looting.

Meanwhile, French left-wing leader and presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon criticised the police response to the demonstrations in Paris.

In a post on X, Melenchon said, "In Paris, to ruin the day and unwind, the so-called forces of law and order gas and fire into the crowd at the back of the procession, all in a bid to get footage for the domestic news channels that spent the whole week airing the images that spurred the Trappes killer. Nonstop shame."

In another post, he alleged that the media coverage and policing were being used to portray the protest movement negatively.

"It continues with the policing of minds through the televisions of power. Tonight, staging of the « tails of the procession » to spew hatred against the popular movement. Without a single image of the masses in peaceful action," he said.

"Behind every police officer, a compliant camera. And even congratulations for a setup deliberately designed to provoke chaos. And which has yet again mutilated two people," Melenchon added, urging people to "Turn off the televisions!" and "Form your own opinion without a guardian."

US President Donald Trump also commented on the situation in France during a campaign rally in Perry, Georgia, on Saturday (local time).

"France is right now burning down because it opens its borders to people who hate it. These are people who hate it. They hate France. They hate the people of France. They move there. They don't like the buildings. They don't like the monuments. They don't like the paintings. They don't like anything about France. And you know what you do with those people? Never let them come into your country. And that's what we're doing," Trump said.

In Albania, thousands of people gathered in the capital, Tirana, on Saturday for another anti-government protest. Police fired tear gas to disperse demonstrators as clashes continued amid growing opposition involving students, artists and political groups.

According to Euronews, government buildings were attacked, and dozens of demonstrators were detained. Authorities said more than 300 protesters and police personnel had been injured.

In Italy, thousands of demonstrators took to the streets in Milan, Rome, Turin, Naples, Bologna and Florence, with some protesters throwing bottles, stones and firecrackers.

Italian police said they had made nine arrests and briefly detained 371 people during demonstrations in eight cities on Saturday. Of those taken to police stations, 110 were minors, the police statement added.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni thanked law enforcement personnel for maintaining public order and protecting the right to peaceful protest despite attempts by what she described as "violent individuals" to provoke clashes.

In a post on X, Meloni said, "I want to thank the women and men of the Law Enforcement Agencies who, even today, in Italy's squares, have worked to ensure the safety of citizens and the right to peaceful demonstration, despite the attempts by some violent individuals to provoke clashes and disorder."

She also thanked Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi, prefects, questors and others involved in coordinating security operations.

"The right to demonstrate must always be guaranteed, just as the right of citizens to live their cities in safety must be," Meloni wrote.

She said measures approved by the Council of Ministers were intended to strengthen the authorities' ability to prevent violence and maintain public safety.

"Because safety must be guaranteed to everyone. To those who want to demonstrate peacefully, to those who work, and to those who want to live their city without fear. Without leaving room for those who seek only confrontation and violence," she added.

In Spain, demonstrators in Madrid called for pension increases to be linked to actual inflation, higher minimum pensions in line with the minimum wage, measures to close the gender pension gap and safeguards against the privatisation of the public pension system.

In Portugal, affordable housing emerged as a central demand, with demonstrators taking to the streets amid concerns over housing costs. (ANI)

news.title: US Fed expected to hold rates as inflation, energy costs weigh ahead of midterms
news.text: The US Federal Reserve is widely expected to keep interest rates unchanged at its meeting next week, despite persistent inflation and market expectations of at least one more rate hike before the end of the year, according to analysts cited by news agency AFP.The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) will meet over two days, with its interest rate decision scheduled for 2 pm local time (1800 GMT) on Wednesday.At its September meeting, the Fed raised its benchmark federal funds rate for the first time in three years, taking the target range to 3.75%-4%. The central bank has struggled to bring inflation down to its long-term target of 2%, which it has missed for more than five years.The decision comes just days before the November 3 US midterm elections, in which Democrats are seeking to wrest control of both chambers of Congress from President Donald Trump's Republican Party.Inflation pressures complicate Fed's rate decisionThe Fed's preferred inflation gauge, the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, reached a pandemic-era peak of 7.2% in 2022 before a series of interest rate increases brought it down to around 2.2% by late 2024.However, inflation subsequently rose again amid Trump's economic policies, including tariffs that disrupted global trade and the US war with Iran. The PCE index reached a three-year high of 3.9% in May.Since the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February, global energy prices have surged, with retaliatory actions by Tehran sharply restricting oil and gas supplies through the Gulf. Higher energy costs have also begun feeding into the prices of other goods and services, putting affordability at the forefront of concerns ahead of the midterm elections.The Fed faces the challenge of controlling inflation while supporting the labour market. Higher interest rates increase borrowing costs, potentially slowing economic activity and curbing price pressures, but they can also weigh on employment.The US economy has also been dealing with weakening consumer confidence and signs of stress in an otherwise resilient jobs market. The latest consumer confidence survey from the Conference Board was expected to show a further decline in October after confidence fell in September to its lowest level in more than a decade.Former Fed official says economic data favour further hikesLoretta Mester, a former president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, told AFP that the timing of the meeting ahead of the elections would not influence policymakers' decision."The Fed doesn't take into account any kind of political issues in that FOMC room," she said. "It really is based on the economics."Mester argued that economic conditions supported further monetary tightening, pointing to a stable labour market and inflation remaining above the central bank's target."The data that's come in continue to show a stable labor market and continue to show inflation above target," she said, adding that there was no evidence of inflation moving towards the target."The economics would suggest then you need to continue raising rates."However, Mester said most policymakers appeared reluctant to move too quickly. She expected the Fed could hold rates steady in October and consider another increase at its next meeting in early December.Wendy Edelberg, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, also said that central bankers would prefer to avoid becoming part of the political debate ahead of the elections."It's unhelpful for everyone if the Fed gets wrapped up in all the political discourse right before an election," she said.Edelberg added that raising rates in December rather than October would have limited economic implications.She viewed a possible delay less as a concession to Trump, who has repeatedly called for lower interest rates, and more as a way for the Fed to avoid becoming a target of political criticism.Trump's criticism of Fed independenceTrump has repeatedly criticised the Federal Reserve over interest rates, which he considers too high. However, he has so far refrained from directing similar criticism at Kevin Warsh, whom he appointed to succeed Jerome Powell as Fed chair.Since returning to power last year, Trump has mounted an unprecedented challenge to the central bank's independence. His administration launched a criminal investigation into Powell and attempted to remove Fed Governor Lisa Cook.The investigation into Powell was dropped to smooth the way for Warsh's confirmation by the Senate, while the legal battle over Cook's removal continued despite a Supreme Court decision nullifying an earlier attempt to dismiss her.Last week, Cook declined to attend a hearing in a White House investigation into mortgage fraud allegations, which she denies.Meanwhile, the Fed's rate decision will come during a busy week for US economic data.Investors and policymakers were also awaiting updates on inflation, consumer confidence and third-quarter economic growth, alongside earnings reports from major companies.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
news.summary: The US Federal Reserve is expected to keep interest rates unchanged in its upcoming meeting next week. Analysts suggest this decision comes despite ongoing inflation pressures and looming midterm elections. The Federal Reserve has struggled to meet its long-term inflation target due to rising prices affecting multiple sectors. Heightened energy costs after global conflicts are contributing significantly to inflation pressures.

news.title: Musk says he was behind Starlink speed curbs after Ukraine service restored
news.text: Ukraine's access to Starlink and Starshield satellite links has been restored to the speeds it had before restrictions that disrupted front-line operations for more than a week, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday."The speeds are now where they need to be," Zelenskyy wrote on X, adding that restoration began overnight and were sufficient by Saturday morning, improving front-line logistics and defence against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones.Musk admits he was behind Starlink's speed restrictionAfter Ukraine said the services had been restored, Elon Musk spoke out on the speed restrictions that began last week. In a post on Saturday on X, Musk acknowledged that his company, SpaceX, throttled the Starlink satellite internet service."Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote. "Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week." But he maintained that the US government controlled whatever changes happened with Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink that is the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and communication. He also defended the role of SpaceX in bolstering Ukraine's defences since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.Restrictions imposed last week on Starshield alarmed the country's military and government officials, with commanders reporting lost drones and disrupted missions.The restoration follows a new US diplomatic push to end the war. Russia agreed on Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv next month. On Friday, Kyiv and Moscow also agreed to a localised ceasefire brokered by first lady Melania Trump around Oleshky, a war-ravaged, Russian-occupied town in Ukraine's southern Kherson region.Restriction led to tensions between Ukraine and the USThe episode added to tensions between Kyiv and Washington, a relationship already strained by President Donald Trump's reported deal with Moscow on Russian diesel imports, which Ukraine viewed as a betrayal.Ukraine's Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara credited "direct dialogue" and Zelenskyy's diplomacy with Washington, adding that the outcome mattered most "for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics and communications".Questions have persisted since last week about who ordered the interruptions to the Elon Musk-made satellite internet system that Ukraine has relied on for years to counter Moscow's attacks.Trump has maintained that he did not make the call, while also saying Musk should not be blamed. Vice President J D Vance has hinted at White House coordination with Musk, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth have denied any administration involvement.Russia and Ukraine have continued to target each otherMeanwhile, a man was killed and two others were wounded in a missile attack on the city of Lozova in Ukraine's Kharkiv region, local officials said on Saturday.Moscow-installed authorities in cities across Russia-occupied Crimea reported power blackouts on Saturday following overnight Ukrainian attacks.Ukraine's General Staff said on Saturday that its forces hit a chemical plant in the Russian city of Tolyatti, which produces materials used in rocket fuel. Tolyatti Mayor Ilya Sukhikh said the overnight attack damaged industrial facilities in the city.Ukrainian forces also hit an electronics plant in the city of Oryol, Ukraine's General Staff confirmed on Saturday. Local officials in Oryol said on Saturday that three people were killed in Friday's attack. The General Staff said the plant makes components for the cruise and ballistic missiles Russia fires at Ukrainian cities.Ukrainian drones also reached Russia's Omsk region in western Siberia, more than 2,000 kilometres (1,242 miles) from the border with Ukraine. Omsk regional Governor Vitaly Khotsenko said drones "reached a northern industrial hub".Online retailer Ozon said on Saturday that its logistics centre in Omsk has been attacked by a drone, but there were no casualties. Ozon is a competitor to Wildberries, whose facilities Ukraine has also targeted.

news.title: Desperate MAGA Candidate Hit by New Embarrassment Over Vile Ad
news.text:
Vivek Ramaswamy has quietly edited his controversial attack ad targeting Democratic rival Amy Acton, removing her estranged mother’s accusations that she lied about being homeless as a child.

Days after President Donald Trump urged him not to take the ad down, the MAGA gubernatorial candidate released a new 30-second version of the original 60-second spot amid scathing bipartisan criticism.

The shift came hours before Acton appeared onstage with Barack Obama in Cleveland, where the former president delivered a scorched-earth rebuke of Ramaswamy, saying there was almost nothing he wouldn’t do to get into the limelight.

“There’s got to be something inside you where you just say, ‘No office is worth stooping that low,’” Obama said of the Trump-backed gubernatorial candidate.

The original ad sparked a political firestorm because Acton had not spoken to her mother, Donna Arthur, in decades. Arthur remained with Acton’s stepfather even after he raped her as a child.

The Democrat has also spoken publicly about the difficult childhood she shared with her brother—an experience she recounted again on Saturday. 

The original 60-second ad released by Ramaswamy’s campaign specifically challenged Acton’s account of spending part of her childhood living in a tent, with Arthur saying: 

“I love my daughter, but when I saw her lying about her opponent, it’s not easy for a mother to say this, but Amy has a serious problem.

“She is a liar,” Arthur continued. “She lies about her past. She says she grew up living in a tent. None of that is true. She’s lied her entire life. My daughter needs help, and she can’t help you if she needs help herself. People can change, but first they have to tell the truth. And my daughter still isn’t doing that.”

But the new version omits those specific allegations about Acton’s childhood, instead featuring Arthur saying: “I love my daughter, and Amy is a liar. I saw her lying about her opponent. That’s why I’m speaking up to you now. Don’t vote for people who lie. Don’t let her become your governor. If you think she’ll make your life better, you’re fooling yourself. It will only get worse.”

Ramaswamy’s campaign did not respond to questions from the Daily Beast about the edited ad on Saturday, one day after the gubernatorial hopeful spent much of Friday insisting he had done nothing wrong.

“Our ad was about a consistent track record of Amy Acton telling lies, including during this campaign,” he said, criticizing the media for not failing to cover what he described as lies she had told about him and his family. 

Trump and Vice President JD Vance also backed Ramaswamy, despite the controversy surrounding Acton’s childhood abuse.

Many other Republicans, however, urged Ramaswamy to reverse course, warning that the backlash could also affect their must-win Senate race in Ohio between former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown and Republican incumbent/former college football player/object of Trump’s affection, Jon Husted.

“I wouldn’t have told him to put out that ad,” Henry Nickel, who has been knocking on doors for the GOP for weeks, told the Daily Beast in Ohio.

Some Republicans even declared they would vote for neither Ramaswamy nor Acton, potentially undermining the very goal of Trump’s rallies: turning out the Republican vote. 

“If one must sell one’s soul and reject decency to be elected to office in Ohio, then I praise my Savior and Protector that @OhioGOP pushed Dave out of the race a year before the primary,” said Darlene Yost, the wife of former Ohio Attorney General Dave Yost, who had sought the Republican gubernatorial nomination.

“Lord forgive us, and save our republic,” she said.

Acton, 60, served as Ohio’s top health official under Republican Gov. Mike DeWine and regularly appeared alongside him for televised updates during the COVID-19 pandemic.

DeWine has since endorsed Ramaswamy to succeed him but called the ad “deeply, deeply troubling” and urged the campaign to take it down.

“You probably heard by now, as a young child, my brother and I experienced a lot of child abuse and neglect,” Acton told the near-capacity crowd in Cleveland on Saturday as they cheered her on.

“We moved countless times as kids, and even wound up living in a tent in the middle of winter,” she continued. “And now my opponent has chosen to intentionally exploit my childhood to save his struggling campaign—but it’s not going to work.”

The latest polls put Acton ahead of Ramaswamy. But at the Circleville Pumpkin Show on Friday night, Michael Hicks said he was optimistic Republicans would hold on to Ohio, “once the air cleared.” 

“There’s too much lying going on. Who’s telling the truth? Who’s doing what? Let’s get down to the issues,” he said.

Asked which issues he wanted addressed, he replied: “I think the number one issue with me is that the career politicians that are corrupt need term limits, and we need oversight on these guys.”

While Ramaswamy and Acton battle over the increasingly ugly campaign, some Ohio voters say they have more pressing concerns than political mudslinging.

In the former industrial town of East Palestine, Ohio, local resident Jami Wallace said healthcare was her main concern. In 2023, 38 cars from a Norfolk Southern freight train derailed in her town, many carrying hazardous materials including vinyl chloride. 

Three years later, she said residents were still dealing with the long-term health impacts, but felt abandoned by both Republicans and Democrats. 

“I can’t even afford to get my daughter’s cavities filled right now as they want $400 upfront,” she told the Daily Beast.
news.summary:
Michael Swensen / Getty ImagesVivek Ramaswamy has quietly edited his controversial attack ad targeting Democratic rival Amy Acton, removing her estranged mother’s accusations that she lied about being homeless as a child.

Days after President Donald Trump urged him not to take the ad down, the MAGA gubernatorial candidate released a new 30-second version of the original 60-second spot amid scathing bipartisan criticism.

news.title: Trump leaves door open to aides’ pardons
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 25 (IANS) President Donald Trump left open the possibility of pardoning administration officials, saying he wanted to protect innocent people from costly investigations, while maintaining that he had not considered such a move. Speaking to reporters after voting early in Palm Beach, Florida, on Saturday, Trump was asked whether he was considering pardons for junior officials to shield them from congressional inquiries. “So certainly, I haven't thought about it, but certainly I'd be allowed to,” he said. “Well, I haven't thought of it, but I will tell you, it would be very unfair to go through what we went through for four years, with the corrupt weaponization that took place,” Trump said. His description of those investigations as corrupt was a political allegation. Trump invoked Biden’s use of pardons, including protections for people involved in the congressional investigation of the January 6, 2021, attack on the US Capitol. He criticised the committee and argued that Biden’s actions provided a precedent for protecting others. But he did not confirm the reporter’s premise that his administration was developing a plan. When another reporter tried to move to Ukraine, Trump continued discussing pardons and the financial consequences of becoming an investigative target. “The, the presidential pardons are, they say the most powerful thing a president has,” he said. His remarks framed possible clemency as protection for people he considered innocent, rather than a response to a specified conviction or charge. The comments came as Trump discussed his campaigning ahead of the midterm elections. Asked separately about working with Democrats if they gained control of either chamber of Congress, he said he wanted to preserve his administration’s legislative achievements and expressed confidence in his campaign efforts.

news.title: US carrier rearms as Iran trade routes narrow: Report
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 25 (IANS) A US aircraft carrier is replenishing supplies for possible renewed strikes against Iran, while restrictions at Iraqi and Pakistani border crossings are adding to Tehran’s economic isolation, according to reports by The Wall Street Journal. The reports describe military preparations and restrictions on commerce as President Donald Trump weighs further action against Iran. Neither establishes that he has issued an order for a new bombing campaign. In a video report published on Saturday, the Journal’s Shelby Holliday described night-time aircraft launches and recoveries aboard USS George Washington in the Arabian Sea, followed by a major replenishment operation. The report said aircraft were enforcing the blockade of Iranian ports and protecting shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. It described the replenishment as indicating preparations for a potentially larger bombing campaign. The Washington Post separately reported preparations to position up to three aircraft carriers and escort vessels in the region in November, citing unnamed officials. On land, Iraq closed the Sheeb crossing on Wednesday, citing anti-smuggling enforcement, the Journal reported. Pakistan restricted Iranian trucks at Gabd and Taftan during the preceding weekend, citing security concerns. Those restrictions predated the Journal’s Friday report and Saturday print edition. They were not announced as new closures on Saturday. Trump, speaking after voting early in Palm Beach, Florida, on Saturday, again left open both military action and an agreement with Tehran. “I may have to finish it off or maybe they'll make a deal, but I'm not sure,” he said. Asked later about the timing of a possible attack, Trump declined to disclose his thinking. He said an attack remained possible, as did an agreement, while questioning whether Iran would honour a deal. He announced neither a military timetable nor a negotiated settlement during the exchange. Meanwhile, The New York Times reported that US agencies assessed threats against Americans in the Middle East and several other countries as their highest since the war began. The newspaper cited unnamed US officials. Its report described potential targets in Europe and intelligence suggesting Iran might have operatives in the United States. Another official, however, cautioned that Iran’s ability to conduct overseas attacks was limited and fell short of its ambitions. Those assessments were not independently verified. The warning was conveyed in an October 23 memo from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to Secretary of State Marco Rubio. A US official had previously confirmed the memo and said threats from Iran and Yemen’s Houthi forces were informing embassy staffing decisions. “When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment,” the official said. The conflict began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February, followed by Iranian attacks across the region. Washington subsequently maintained a blockade of Iranian ports while diplomatic efforts continued.

news.title: 'Tariffs Bring In Jobs': Trump Defends Protectionist Policy With Massive $4.2B Audi Deal
news.text: President Donald Trump defended his decision to wield tariffs during a campaign rally in Georgia, saying they've made the US richer as he announced that Volkswagen AG agreed to build a new $4.2 billion Audi plant in the state.“Think of that. 200,000 cars a year. That's incredible,” Trump told a crowd in the city of Perry. “This will be the single largest investment in U.S. auto industry history, modern history.”Later, he added, “Without tariffs, they wouldn't be coming in.”Trump was speaking as Republicans are trying to flip a Senate seat held by Democrat Jon Ossoff in the midterm elections, despite trailing in the polls.The campaign stop marked Trump's second in the state in as many weeks, an indication of the importance of the Senate contest in Georgia. With less than two weeks until Election Day on Nov. 3, though, Representative Mike Collins, the Republican candidate, faces an uphill battle in a state that was once a GOP stronghold. The RealClearPolitics average of polls has Ossoff leading by more than eight percentage points, while the nonpartisan Cook Political Report has forecast the race as “likely Democrat.”That dynamic is indicative of a broader political climate that has soured for Republican candidates. Trump is at historic low approval ratings and his efforts to tout manufacturing investment promises have failed to resonate with voters who are more concerned with high costs of living and wage growth. The war in Iran has also spiked energy prices, adding further strain to household budgets.The Audi announcement marks a political win for Trump, who has been on the defensive about the domestic effects of his tariffs, particularly on inflation, in a number of battleground Senate races.Bloomberg News reported earlier that Volkswagen plans to manufacture the Audi Q7, Q8 and Q9 models at the Georgia plant, according to a US official involved in the talks.Volkswagen will also expand its Scout Motors plant under construction in Blythewood, South Carolina, adding 25,000 units per year of capacity for a model yet to be determined, said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to detail the plans. Audi said in a news release that the $4 billion plant would create some 4,500 jobs with an annual capacity of up to 200,000 vehicles. Construction will begin next year, with the aim of beginning vehicle production in the early 2030s. “We are planning to bring our biggest and most premium SUVs and produce them here in Macon, Georgia,” Audi Chairman of the Board of Management Gernot Döllner said at the rally, standing near Trump. “This is a long-term investment because we believe in the American market.”Richard Motes, 61, a Perry resident who used to work at an aircraft manufacturer, praised the Audi plant announcement.“That's awesome, I want jobs to come to Georgia,” Motes said. “I'm dead red,” he added. “If they let me push a button to vote all Republican, I'd push the button.”Trump has been traveling nearly daily in the run-up to the midterms, seeking to help boost Republicans in competitive races across the country. Polls indicate Democrats are likely to regain control of the House, but the Senate is still in play with Republicans on the defensive in unexpected states such as Texas and Ohio.Another rally attendee, Chris Capp, 55, a former Army National Guard employee, said he's 50-50 on whether Trump is still an asset to Republican candidates in Georgia, given his falling popularity.“I love Trump to death, but sometimes he should keep his mouth shut,” he said.Earlier: Trump in Georgia Touts Manufacturing Gains as GOP Targets OssoffGeorgia is also home to a a competitive governor's race between Democratic candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican Rick Jackson, which the Cook report has rated a toss-up.Former President Barack Obama is expected to campaign in Georgia with Ossoff and Bottoms on Wednesday. While Ossoff has pledged to serve a full six-year Senate term if reelected, he's been seen as a potential Democratic 2028 contender.Trump won Georgia in 2024 and 2016, but lost to former President Joe Biden in 2020, prompting the president to promote unfounded theories of fraud in that election. Trump pressured Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger to “find” the votes he needed to win the state. Trump and allies were indicted to face allegations of carrying out election interference, but those charges were eventually dropped.The president has repeatedly promoted false claims that he won the 2020 election and questioned the integrity of Georgia's voting counting. Raffensperger earlier this month told Bloomberg Television that he expects the state's election results by midnight on Election Day, downplaying the president's remarks.
news.summary: Trump was speaking as Republicans are trying to flip a Senate seat held by Democrat Jon Ossoff in the midterm elections, despite trailing in the polls.

news.title: Lula's comeback bid vs Bolsonaro's son: Brazil votes in high-stakes run-off
news.text: Brazilian voters are set to cast their ballots on Sunday in a tightly contested presidential run-off between incumbent left-wing leader Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, 80, and right-wing senator Flávio Bolsonaro, 45.Lula is seeking a fourth, non-consecutive term as president, while Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, is attempting to secure the top office. His father is serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election, according to BBC report.Bolsonaro enters the final round with momentum after finishing ahead of Lula in the first round of voting on October 4. US President Donald Trump described that result as a “very big” victory.No candidate who has finished behind their rival in the first round has ever managed to overturn the deficit and win Brazil's presidential run-off.Bolsonaro supporters call for changeSupporters of Flávio Bolsonaro expressed confidence at his final campaign rallies, backing his promises to tackle organised crime through tougher measures, reduce taxes and cut public spending.On the eve of the election, Bolsonaro campaigned in Belo Horizonte, the capital of Minas Gerais. The state has been considered crucial for presidential candidates since the 1980s.“The time is almost here,” Bolsonaro said in a video posted on social media.“There are only a few hours left before we shape the future of our nation for the next 30 or 40 years,” he added.He has also pledged to secure the release of his father, who is serving his sentence under house arrest because of health problems.In Rio de Janeiro's Barra de Tijuca neighbourhood, where Jair Bolsonaro owns a home, supporters gathered wearing Brazil's national colours to demonstrate their backing for the senator.One supporter told BBC News that the country needed a change in leadership and described Flávio Bolsonaro as the candidate capable of delivering it after years of what the supporter called left-wing economic mismanagement.Another supporter said she was drawn to his promises to curb violence, tackle terrorism and drug trafficking, and bring down interest rates.Lula rallies supporters around national sovereigntyFollowing Bolsonaro's first-round lead, Lula's supporters have organised large rallies in an effort to mobilise voters and increase turnout. Around 33 million people did not vote in the first round earlier this month.Addressing a large gathering on Rio de Janeiro's Copacabana beach on Saturday, Lula framed the election as a question of national sovereignty. He said voters would have to choose between a leader who embraced Brazil's flag and one who embraced the American flag.Lula's government has accused the United States of interfering in Brazil's election, a charge Washington has dismissed as “baseless”.“We're going to win the election for one simple reason: it's true that the people want change [but] they want to move forward,” Lula told the crowd. “They don't want to go backward.”A Lula supporter, Roberta, told BBC News that the rallies were intended to demonstrate the movement's strength and encourage people to take to the streets to help reverse the first-round result.Another supporter, wearing Brazil's iconic yellow and green football shirt, said Bolsonaro's supporters had “appropriated” the national jersey, but Lula's backers were now reclaiming it.You use AI every day. news.summary: Brazil gears up for a thrilling presidential run-off featuring incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva against challenger Flávio Bolsonaro. Despite Bolsonaro's lead in the first round, Lula's vibrant rallies aim to rally supporters and boost voter turnout. Bolsonaro focuses on tackling crime and economic reform, while Lula champions national dignity and promises transformative progress. This election could reshape Brazil's future, with millions poised to make their voices heard.

news.title: Trump backs local approval for data centres
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 25 (IANS) President Donald Trump backed local approval of data centres and said communities hosting them should receive substantial financial benefits, while arguing that the United States needs the facilities to compete with China. Speaking to WANF-TV’s Atlanta News First before a rally in Perry, Georgia, on Saturday, Trump rejected the suggestion that he differed with Republican gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson over whether local communities should approve such projects. “I agree with that. No, I agree with that. And I think locals should be paid a lot of money for data centers,” Trump told interviewer Abby Kousouris. His response endorsed a local role in decisions on data centres, but he did not outline an approval process or announce a federal measure to establish one. He also did not explain how payments to communities would be calculated or distributed. Kousouris raised the issue by saying Jackson believed local residents should be able to approve data centres. Trump responded by arguing that financial benefits could change how communities viewed the facilities. “When a data center goes in, I've seen it. People are very unhappy. All of a sudden, a data center decides to pay a community, uh, in the form of taxes, in a form of whatever. And all of a sudden, the same people love what they're doing,” he said. He coupled his support for local benefits with an argument for continued construction, citing competition with China. Trump said China was building data centres rapidly and asserted that the United States was ahead, without offering a measure for that comparison. “But the data centers, they have money. They can pay local communities a lot,” he said. Asked whether he and Jackson had discussed particular regulations, or differed over them, Trump did not identify a specific proposal. Instead, he returned to the possibility of payments resembling a tax or dividend. He predicted that such benefits would make residents more receptive to data centres. He did not specify whether money would go to local governments, individual households or both, and gave no timetable for introducing a payment arrangement. Trump also said the facilities would provide their own electricity and supply power to the grid. He did not name any projects or provide details of their generating capacity during the interview. “So the data centers are gonna be fine, but let the people benefit from the data centers,” he said. His remarks expressed support for community consent and compensation without setting out new regulatory requirements. The White House’s March 4 Ratepayer Protection Pledge called on participating technology companies to cover the additional electricity supply and infrastructure required by their data centres. It also included commitments to local hiring, workforce training and coordination with grid operators. Those commitments concern company practices and do not themselves demonstrate that household electricity costs have fallen. Data centres support services including cloud computing and artificial intelligence. Their servers require dependable electricity and cooling to operate continuously. The US Department of Energy identifies both power supply and the removal of heat from computing equipment as central requirements of these facilities.

news.title: 'Ukraine Violated Starlink, Used It To Kill People': Elon Musk As Speed Restores
news.text: Elon Musk said on Saturday that his company SpaceX had throttled the Starlink satellite internet service in Ukraine, disrupting operations that the country relies on to defend itself against Russia.Musk's admission on social media came after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine's access to Starlink and Starshield satellite links has been restored to the speeds it had before restrictions that disrupted front-line operations for more than a week.Questions have persisted since last week about who ordered the interruptions to the Musk-made satellite internet system that Kyiv has relied on for years to counter Moscow's attacks."The speeds are now where they need to be," Zelenskyy wrote on X, adding that restoration began overnight and were sufficient by Saturday morning, improving front-line logistics and defense against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones.After Ukraine said the services had been restored, Elon Musk spoke out on the speed restrictions that began last week. In a post Saturday on X, Musk acknowledged that his company SpaceX throttled the Starlink satellite internet service."Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote. "Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week."But he maintained that the US government controlled whatever changes happened with Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink that is the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and communication. He also defended the role of SpaceX in bolstering Ukraine's defenses since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.Restrictions imposed last week on Starshield alarmed the country's military and government officials, with commanders reporting lost drones and disrupted missions.The restoration follows a new US diplomatic push to end the war. Russia agreed Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv next month. On Friday, Kyiv and Moscow also agreed to a localized ceasefire brokered by first lady Melania Trump around Oleshky, a war-ravaged, Russian-occupied town in Ukraine's southern Kherson region.The episode added to tensions between Kyiv and Washington, a relationship already strained by President Donald Trump's reported deal with Moscow on Russian diesel imports, which Ukraine viewed as a betrayal.Ukraine's Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara credited "direct dialogue" and Zelenskyy's diplomacy with Washington, adding that the outcome mattered most "for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics and communications."Trump has maintained that he didn't make the call, while also saying Musk should not be blamed. Vice President JD Vance has hinted at White House coordination with Musk, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth have denied any administration involvement.Meanwhile, a man was killed and two others wounded in a missile attack on the city of Lozova in Ukraine's Kharkiv region, local officials said Saturday.Moscow-installed authorities in cities across Russia-occupied Crimea reported power blackouts Saturday following overnight Ukrainian attacks.Ukraine's General Staff said Saturday that its forces hit a chemical plant in the Russian city of Tolyatti, which produces materials used in rocket fuel. Tolyatti Mayor Ilya Sukhikh said the overnight attack damaged industrial facilities in the city.Ukrainian forces also hit an electronics plant in the city of Oryol, Ukraine's General Staff confirmed Saturday. Local officials in Oryol said Saturday that three people were killed in Friday's attack. The General Staff said the plant makes components for the cruise and ballistic missiles Russia fires at Ukrainian cities.Ukrainian drones also reached Russia's Omsk region in western Siberia, more than 2,000 kilometers (1,242 miles) from the border with Ukraine. Omsk regional Gov. Vitaly Khotsenko said drones "reached a northern industrial hub."Online retailer Ozon said Saturday that its logistics center in Omsk has been attacked by a drone, but there were no casualties. Ozon is a competitor to Wildberries, whose facilities Ukraine has also targeted.(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)

news.title: Andy Burnham wants 'honest discussion' on EU freedom of movement return
news.text: Andy Burnham said he wants an “honest discussion” about the possibility of a return to free movement between the UK and European Union as part of his plans for a new relationship with the bloc. The Prime Minister wants to consider various options for a new relationship with Brussels, potentially i ncluding a return to full EU membership or joining the single market – which would require free movement . He told the Sunday Times : “I think you have to have a very factual, quite evidence-based debate about this.” The Prime Minister has previously committed to the red lines in Labour’s 2024 election manifesto – which ruled out the return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union – suggesting any fundamental change in the relationship would have to wait until after a general election . The issue of migration was one of the dominant factors during the 2016 Brexit referendum campaign. But he suggested the type of migration experienced during the years of EU membership was different from the challenges faced now. He said: “It was generally younger people, not always, but spending a few years, then going back. And obviously the ease of that worked for British people as well.” Mr Burnham will meet the European Union’s chiefs at a summit on November 20 in Brussels. He has said he will take the opportunity around the summit to lay out to the British public different options for the future relationship with the bloc. The Prime Minister acknowledged freedom of movement “had very significant challenges associated with it and I spoke about them in my previous time in parliament”. “But at the same time, it was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult (as now)," he added. “Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different. The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.” But Mr Burnham said he could not imagine recommending the UK joins the Schengen borderless area or ditches the pound to adopt the euro, he added: “I can’t see myself ever recommending anything that would involve joining the euro or Schengen." Nigel Farage said the comments were a betrayal of voters who backed Brexit, including in Mr Burnham’s Makerfield constituency. The Reform UK leader said: “This is a total betrayal of Brexit Britain and his Makerfield pitch. He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty.” Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said: “ Andy Burnham knows full well that a return to EU free movement would mean handing back control of our borders and allowing uncontrolled migration from across Europe. The British people voted to end free movement, and there can be no return to it.” The Sunday Times conducted a series of interviews with Mr Burnham in the in the run-up to his 100th day in office on Tuesday. “Three months in, I’ve got the measure of it now,” Mr Burnham said. “I know the tram lines. I’ve got to be radical, but disciplined. I’ve got to be connected on the ground, but sufficiently detached in a way. I’ve got to balance some opposites. I know a lot is riding on it. ” Mr Burnham revealed he had “connected” with US president Donald Trump “more than I imagined”. “Like me, he will happily divert onto sport for a good 20 minutes,” he said. “ Golf , in his case.” He said they had “many differences” but “there’s something about a more instinctive approach … The over-calculation of politics is what puts the public off”. The Prime Minister also said he took strength from his Catholic faith. Asked if he prays or leant on the faith for guidance, he said “it’s looser” than that. “I wouldn’t want to overemphasise it but it’s all still there inside, if I could put it that way. It can never not be there. I do take strength from it. My dad’s funeral was at the same church where I was an altar boy. You go back and you feel the pull of it all.”
news.summary: The Prime Minister has already touted closer relations with Europe - including opening the door to rejoining the EU - and now says he wants an 'honest discussion' on freedom of movement
news.author: Ethan Davies

news.title: Ilhan Omar hires Joe Biden's pricey personal attorney days after begging supporters for cash to pay her legal fees
news.text:
Embattled Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar has enlisted former President Joe Biden's personal attorney to help fight a mounting federal investigation into her finances and immigration history.

The Minnesota congresswoman has assembled a heavyweight legal team featuring two Washington attorneys with extensive experience battling President Donald Trump.

Investigators are currently scrutinizing allegations surrounding her past and her husband's reported $30 million fortune.

Among those now representing Omar is Amy Jeffress, the high-profile lawyer who defended Biden during investigations into his controversial use of an autopen to authorize presidential documents.

She has been joined by Joshua Matz, another prominent attorney who helped House Democrats pursue both of Trump's impeachments.

Both lawyers are partners at the Washington-based firm Hecker Fink, bringing formidable political and legal experience to Omar's defense as she faces one of the most serious controversies of her congressional career.

Their involvement comes just days after Omar, 44, appeared in a fundraising video filmed inside a moving vehicle, warning supporters that her legal fight would be costly.

'It is going to be a very expensive and challenging time and so we appreciate whether you're able to send $5, $10, $20,' she said on Tuesday night.

The appeal has attracted attention given Omar's $174,000 congressional salary and recent financial disclosures indicating that assets associated with her husband, political consultant Tim Mynett, could be worth tens of millions of dollars.

Despite those figures, Omar insisted during an interview with MS NOW that she lives 'paycheck to paycheck.'

The New York Post reported that campaign finance records filed through October 15 showed no payments directly to Jeffress, Matz or their law firm.

Jeffress brings an extensive résumé to the case, having taken over as Biden's personal attorney in 2025 from his longtime legal adviser Bob Bauer.

She represented the former president as federal authorities examined his administration's use of an autopen to sign pardons and other official documents.

Before joining Hecker Fink, Jeffress worked at the prestigious Washington law firm Arnold & Porter and became involved in several politically charged congressional investigations.

She served as outside counsel to the House committee investigating the January 6, 2021, Capitol riot, assisting its efforts to obtain testimony and documents through subpoenas.

Omar's second attorney, Matz, also has a notable history of legal clashes involving Trump.

He represented House Democrats during both impeachment proceedings against the president and also worked with the January 6 committee.

His other clients have included Brown University, New York University and Columbia University, institutions that have faced legal confrontations with the Trump administration.

Neither attorney primarily specializes in immigration law, according to the Post, although their experience in congressional investigations and high-stakes constitutional disputes could prove valuable to Omar.

Their recruitment comes as federal prosecutors in Washington examine questions involving the congresswoman's immigration background and financial disclosures.

Particular attention has focused on Omar's marriage history, including longstanding, unproven allegations that her former husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, was actually her brother.

The accusation, which originated years ago on a Somali-language blog, has repeatedly been denied by Omar. No court has established that she married a sibling or committed immigration fraud.

Investigators have also reportedly examined her financial filings, which have undergone revisions amid congressional scrutiny of her husband's business interests.

Questions surrounding Mynett's reported wealth have intensified after disclosures suggested that businesses linked to him could be valued at up to $30 million.

Omar's legal difficulties escalated earlier this month when federal agents searched her Washington, DC, residence and seized personal property.

The congresswoman subsequently complained that she was prevented from contacting her attorney for around an hour following the search.

Court documents associated with the operation reportedly referenced the name Nur Said Elmi, adding to speculation about investigators' interest in her immigration records. 

On Friday, Jeffress and Matz sent a seven-page letter to the Department of Justice demanding the return of Omar's passport, electronic devices and other property taken during the search.

Trump, meanwhile, has shown little inclination to ease the pressure on one of his fiercest Democratic critics.

On Saturday night, the president publicly demanded that Omar 'immediately' resign from Congress, alleging that she had been sworn into office under a name other than her own.
news.summary: Ilhan Omar has hired Joe Biden's former personal attorney Amy Jeffress and Trump impeachment lawyer Joshua Matz as she battles investigations into her finances and immigration history.

news.title: IN BRIEF: Brazil to hold second round of presidential elections
news.text:
RIO DE JANEIRO, October 25. /TASS/. The second, decisive round of the general election will take place in Brazil. Voters will decide who will serve as head of state for the next four years: incumbent President and Workers’ Party leader Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva or the candidate from the right-wing opposition, senator Flavio Bolsonaro.

Voting procedure

Voting in Brazil will take place from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. local time (11:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. GMT). More than 158.7 million Brazilian citizens are eligible to vote. Voting is mandatory for all literate Brazilians between the ages of 18 and 69.

Key candidates

Incumbent President Lula da Silva is seeking re-election for what would be the final term of his political career. He is building his campaign around strengthening Brazil’s international standing and expanding export opportunities, particularly with countries in the Global South and the BRICS. His domestic policy agenda includes tax reform, government funding for defense and technology initiatives, and actively developing hydrocarbon reserves.

Meanwhile, Flavio Bolsonaro is focusing his campaign on strongly condemning the government’s policies and drawing public attention to the excessive tax burden and rampant street crime. The right-wing opposition candidate has rallied the conservative electorate and powerful agricultural interests behind him. In foreign policy, he favors the US market and aims to restore bilateral relations to the level seen during the administrations of Jair Bolsonaro and Donald Trump.

First-round results, political landscape

The October 4 vote showed an advantage for conservative forces and fell short of the incumbent president’s expectations, falling short of the incumbent president’s expectations of a first-round victory. According to the results, Flavio Bolsonaro took the lead with 47.03% of the vote. Lula da Silva is in second place with 45.16%. The margin between the candidates was less than two percentage points. Given an electorate of 150 million, this is equal to nearly two to three million votes.

On the eve of the second round, the son of the former Brazilian leader is considered the frontrunner. Flavio Bolsonaro managed to seize the political initiative by successfully mobilizing voters in economically developed regions and the agricultural business sector.

Lula da Silva’s campaign shifted to a defensive strategy between the rounds, finding itself playing catch-up. The government passed emergency social measures, including debt relief for four million self-employed individuals and an unexpected increase in benefits for the poor.
news.summary: More than 158.7 million Brazilian citizens are eligible to vote
news.author: Tass

news.title: 'Lie and fabrication': Iran denies Hormuz deal offer to US through Pakistan
news.text: Iran has denied reports that it offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in return for the US lifting its naval blockade, with the IRGC-affiliated Tasnim news agency saying Tehran has made no fresh proposal to Pakistani mediators.Citing sources, Tasnim said reports by a Saudi Arabian outlet claiming that Iran had conveyed such an offer to Washington through Pakistan were “a lie and fabrication", Press TV reported.The reports had suggested that Tehran was willing to reopen the strategic waterway if the US ended its naval blockade.On October 18, Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi had said Tehran's proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days remained on the table. He made the remarks while speaking to Iranian media in Baghdad.“Our situation is clear and based on the seven-days proposal presented to ​the ​US. They shared comments which we ⁠are reviewing… If there is any ‌honesty on the US part, which there isn’t, the way to reopening the Strait of Hormuz is obvious,” he said.The denial comes as US President Donald Trump has maintained that a deal with Iran remains possible, while keeping the option of further military action open. He has insisted that any agreement must permanently prevent Tehran from developing nuclear weapons.Trump also threatened fresh military action against Iran if it fails to reach a diplomatic agreement with Washington, suggesting that the US could launch "another little Epic Fury".Speaking at a campaign rally in Florida, Trump adopted a hardline stance towards Tehran, referring to previous US military action and warning that further strikes remained an option if negotiations failed."We may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree," Trump told the cheering crowd.Questioning Iran's willingness to negotiate, he added, "If they're smart, they'll just say, 'Let's get down to business. But, you know, I doubt they'll do that because perhaps they're not smart."Iran claims full control over Strait of HormuzAmid the escalating rhetoric, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) on Saturday claimed that Iran retained full control over the Strait of Hormuz, adding that vessels operating in the region were being provided security in accordance with Iranian regulations.The IRGC Navy also alleged that two supertankers carrying more than 4.5 million barrels of crude oil combined had struck naval mines while attempting to navigate a southern route through the waterway that Tehran described as unauthorised.Iran has separately warned that it would not allow US military vessels to enter the Persian Gulf, pushing back against Washington's claims that Iranian military capabilities had been significantly weakened.According to Iranian state broadcaster Press TV, Major General Ali Abdollahi, chief of the general staff of Iran's armed forces, said Iranian forces had rendered the US Navy ineffective in the region."The US president must only dream of their military and army entering the Persian Gulf again. They will take this wish to their graves," Abdollahi said."We will under no circumstances and at no time allow US military vessels to enter the Persian Gulf," he added.Abdollahi also challenged Trump's repeated assertions that Iran's nuclear facilities had been destroyed, questioning why Washington continued to express concerns over Tehran's nuclear programme if the facilities had already been eliminated.You use AI every day. news.title: Andy Burnham touts possible return to free movement between UK and EU as he says he wants 'honest discussion'
news.text:
Andy Burnham has suggested a possible return to free movement between the UK and the European Union. 

The Prime Minister said he wants an 'honest discussion' with the EU as part of his plans for a renewed relationship with the bloc.

Mr Burnham is considering a variety of options to cosy up to Brussels which could include rejoining the EU and the single market.

The decision to move closer to the EU was announced at the Labour Party Conference last month but it has not yet been decided how they will do so. 

The PM previously committed to the red lines in Labour's 2024 election manifesto which ruled out fundamental changes including a return to the EU until after a general election. 

But the PM suggested that migration today is far different from the challenges faced when the UK was in the EU. 

Free movement allowed any EU citizen to move to the UK and was widely viewed as the main reason the UK left Europe after the 2016 Brexit Referendum.

He said that at the time, it generally consisted of younger people staying for a few years before moving back to their home nation.

'Obviously the ease of that worked for British people as well,' he told The Times.

Mr Burnham will meet with the European Union's chiefs at a summit in Brussels on November 20.

Ahead of the summit, he said he would set out the potential options for a relationship with the EU to the public.

The PM also acknowledged freedom of movement 'had very significant challenges associated with it and I spoke about them in my previous time in parliament'. 

'But at the same time, it was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn't as difficult (as now). Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different.'

He added that a conversation about free movement with the EU requires 'a very factual, quite evidence-based debate'.

Despite being keen to bring the UK closer to Europe, Mr Burnham said he does not intend to join the Schengen borderless area. 

Nigel Farage said the comments betrayed voters in favour of leaving the EU including in Mr Burnham's Makerfield constituency. 

The Reform UK leader said: 'This is a total betrayal of Brexit Britain and his Makerfield pitch. 

'He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty.' 

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said: 'Andy Burnham knows full well that a return to EU free movement would mean handing back control of our borders and allowing uncontrolled migration from across Europe. 

'The British people voted to end free movement, and there can be no return to it.'

Mr Burnham revealed he had gotten on with US President Donald Trump better than he imagined.

He said they bonded over being able to have a good chat about sport and golf. 

The potential return to free movement comes after Sadiq Khan ramped up the pressure on Mr Burnham to start reversing Brexit at a summit in November.

The London Mayor insisted the PM must take the opportunity to strike agreements on food and drink standards and a youth 'free movement' scheme.

In a letter to ministers, Lord Khan said such deals would help move the UK towards the 'destination' of rejoining the EU and boost the economy. 

The intervention will fuel fears that the premier could make big concessions in his determination to secure closer ties at the summit in Brussels on November 20.

news.summary: The Prime Minister said he wants an 'honest discussion' with the EU as part of his plans for a renewed relationship with Brussels.
