news.title: Bolsonaro heir could bring Brazil closer to Trump if elected president
news.text:
Brazil's far-right political movement, known as "Bolsonarism", appeared dead in the water less than a year ago.

Former president Jair Bolsonaro, the movement's central figure, had just been found guilty of leading a coup attempt two years prior, and begun serving a 27-year sentence at federal police headquarters. 

But the movement saw a reversal of fortunes at elections at the start of October, with Bolsonaro's wife, two of his sons, and one of his brothers, winning seats in congressional races.

The family's biggest win could still be yet to come, though, as Bolsonaro's eldest son, Flávio, heads to a run-off against leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (known worldwide as Lula), after outperforming expectations in the first round on October 4. 

If he succeeds, Brazil will be the latest Latin American country to lean into a conservative wave that has swept the region since US President Donald Trump returned to office.

A jailed president

A former military paratrooper with a fondness for the brutal military dictatorship that ruled Brazil for 21 years to 1985, Jair Bolsonaro was once considered a "fringe figure" in politics.

He served in Congress for almost 30 years before enjoying a surge in popularity during the 2018 presidential election campaign, off the back of a massive corruption scandal involving the Workers' Party, for which Lula was jailed. 

Jair promised change, with policies such as tax cuts across the board, a crackdown on crime, and reducing government intervention in the economy. It was popular enough to unseat the Workers' Party, which had been in power for 15 years.

Deborah Barros Leal Farias, an associate professor at the University of NSW, said his success was an overlap of two key groups: those who liked Jair as a candidate, and those who wanted the Workers' Party out.

"A lot of people were tired; just wanting something that was different. You had a lot of people who were just willing to say, 'Let's give this a shot,'" she said.

Maintaining popularity once president proved more difficult, and in 2022, Jair lost his re-election bid to Lula, who finished his jail sentence in 2018.

Toward the end of his term, Jair and his close aides began drafting decrees to stay in power and a plot to assassinate the president-elect.

Neither the assassination plot, nor the draft decrees, were successfully executed, but in 2025, Jair was convicted for his involvement, and for inciting riots that occurred the week after Lula's 2023 inauguration.

The next generation

Jair might have been jailed, but the discontentment he once captured had not wavered.

Lula's approval rating was suffering over crime rates and cost of living, some of which could be attributed to excessive spending by the administration.

A large voting block entered the campaign season with one priority: anyone but Lula.

"Even though, for a while, those who loved Bolsonaro weren't as loud, the voice of those who do not want the Workers' Party remained constant," Dr Barros Leal Farias said.

The Bolsonaro clan saw an opportunity for a comeback in Flávio.

He is not without his own corruption allegations, but experts say Flávio pitching himself as an alternative to Lula, and a moderate version of his father, was potent enough for many to look past his previous scandals. 

"Lula's voters look at Bolsonaro's family and associate it with an attempted coup, [and] the behaviour around COVID during the pandemic … [ but] the same happens on the other side," political analyst Thiago de Aragão said. 

"Bolsonaro voters looking at Lula remember when he was arrested, and the corruption scandals.

"This gave very little margin of change from both sides."

The polarisation has left the presidential hopefuls fighting for a very small voting block ahead of the election: about 8 per cent of those who cast votes for now-eliminated candidates in the first round.

Those eliminated candidates were mostly right wing, Mr de Aragão said, meaning many would likely flow to Flávio.

Opinion polls published since the first round of the election suggest Flávio has held a narrow lead over Lula.

The Trump factor

The US has remained publicly neutral during democratic election cycles in Latin America since the Cold War ended.

But it has taken a more active stance in recent years, with Mr Trump publicly endorsing several allied right-wing candidates.

The Trump administration has stated its intention to revive an 1823 policy called the Monroe Doctrine to "restore American [US] pre-eminence in the Western Hemisphere". 

"We want other nations to see us as their partner of first choice, and we will [through various means] discourage their collaboration with others," the document reads.

Mr Trump stopped just short of endorsing Flávio in the Brazilian election but has maintained close public ties with the Bolsonaros.

He met with Flávio at the White House in June and lauded the 45-year-old for his "big victory" of advancing to the runoff against Lula.

The election comes at a time when Brazil wrestles with whether to further align itself with China.

It's a shift many other countries in the region have already pursued as Latin America's so-called "pink tide" recedes and conservative leaders seek friendships with the US.

Dr Barros Leal Farias said a shift right appeared to be the "Zeitgeist" across Latin America. 

"In Latin America for the last 150 years at least, there's been this sense of some governments wanting to get closer to the US because they think that's going to be the best for their country, and others saying, 'No, if we want to really improve our country, we have to move away from the US.'

The conservative shift is something Flávio would continue for Brazil.

"[Brazil's] relationship … with China today is not a positive relationship … because Brazil is excessively dependant on China [absorbing agricultural exports]," Mr de Aragão said.

"What we will see is, Brazil more aligned with the US in terms of narratives, especially narratives against conceptual enemies, as long as China is not one of those."

Interference allegations

Ahead of the first round of voting, Lula and his allies warned of foreign interference in the election, pointing to tariffs, embassy closures, and an effort by Washington to send officials to Brazil to "discuss electoral integrity".

The US suspended consular services on October 2, citing security concerns, though Brazil's federal police said they had found no evidence of security threats.

Edinho Silva, president of Lula's Workers' Party, said the closures were "unprecedented" and made "no sense at all".

"It's one of Trump's ways of trying to influence Brazilian public opinion," he said.

The US Department of State has denied claims of election interference.

Lula's camp has also alleged Meta manipulated social media access to favour the Bolsonaro side, noting that some of its posts appeared without share buttons, suffered reduced reach or appeared without audio.

Meta employees acknowledged in internal communications that Lula's accounts were hindered, according to a report by Folha de S.Paulo.

But the social media giant said the technical issues cited in the report were already publicly known, and "any suggestion that Meta favours one side is false".
news.summary: The son of a disgraced former president hopes to win Brazil's top office at a runoff election this weekend. If he does, it will be a boon for US President Donald Trump.
news.author: Elissa Fitzgerald

news.title: The signs that China's overweight, hard-drinking dictator could be seriously ill - and why the West should be worried: IAN WILLIAMS
news.text:
Officials called it the 'hold room', a private space in the West Wing of the White House set aside for Xi Jinping to take lengthy rest breaks between meetings during last month's summit with Donald Trump. 

The demand for the room was highly unusual, according to US officials, and may hold the secret of a gathering mystery – that of the true state of the Chinese leader's health.

Trump claimed 73–year–old Xi looked 'strong, vibrant and fit', but – privately – officials were struck by his physical weakness.

China demanded a substantial amount of downtime be built into the schedule and were concerned about how long Xi would be required to stand and walk, according to The Wall Street Journal.

One of the main demands was the 'hold room', where only Xi's wife, Peng Liyuan, was allowed to join him. Not even his powerful chief of staff, Cai Qi, was granted entry.

China reportedly turned down an offer of a working lunch with Trump on the only full day of the summit, according to officials involved in planning.

Stairs seemed a particular challenge for Xi. Slowly and cautiously descending from his plane on arrival in Washington – and later climbing the steps of the National Archives – he appeared to be gripping tightly to his wife's hand in a manner that suggested support rather than affection.

Peng, a glamorous singer who gained fame as a soprano for the People's Liberation Army, was more famous than her husband when he first became leader. She has had a much higher profile than the spouses of earlier leaders.

But all the same, the scene in Washington was unusual, since wives have traditionally played a more decorative or ceremonial role – if they had a role at all – in recent Chinese diplomacy.

It could be that Xi was just tired. Perhaps he had jet lag. But Chinese media were taking no chances, editing out any images that might suggest frailty.

State television reports skipped the aircraft steps and instead showed carefully edited video of Xi waving at the cabin door before cutting to the formalities on the tarmac below.

Unsubstantiated rumours about Xi's health were spreading even before the Trump meeting.

At a summit of emerging nations held in New Delhi earlier in September he withdrew at the last minute from a gala dinner hosted by Narendra Modi, the Indian Prime Minister. He reportedly felt unwell, prompting lurid reports spread by overseas exiles that he had fallen seriously ill and been rushed home.

The claim was pushed by Xie Wanjun, one of the dissident founders of the outlawed China Democratic Party, who is now based in the US. Quoting 'witnesses', he claimed that on arrival back in Beijing, Xi was carried off his plane and rushed to hospital by helicopter for emergency treatment.

A series of unexplained absences have also fuelled speculation.

In May last year he disappeared from public view for two weeks and analysts noted a marked reduction in the usual prolific references in state media to 'Xi Jinping Thought'. 

He vanished again at the end of May this year, for ten days this time, and a monthly Politburo meeting appeared to have been scrapped – which is highly unusual.

Caution is required, since the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) is an opaque and paranoid organisation. During my time in Beijing, a diplomat advised me: 'Anybody who claims to understand the party is misinformed.'

It is a system where rumours take on a life of their own and official denials are widely regarded as confirmations of truth.

The CCP even banned all mention of Winnie–the–Pooh from social media after Chinese internet users deployed the rotund bear to mock Xi's physique.

Xi is a lifelong smoker, overweight, unfit and fond of drink, according to Dennis Wilder, a former senior China analyst at the Central Intelligence Agency who is now a scholar at Georgetown University. 

He told The Wall Street Journal about a conversation with Qin Gang, China's former foreign minister, during which Qin said that Xi 'loved to drink'. A favourite tipple was Moutai, a powerful grain liquor popular with China's leaders.

'They would drink themselves silly,' according to Wilder.

Desmond Shum, an exiled but still well–connected Chinese businessman, who had close ties to the family of former Chinese premier Wen Jiabao, says China's leaders go to extraordinary lengths to hide any ill health while travelling internationally.

'We were told they travelled with their own toilets and that even their s**t was packed up and taken away, lest their DNA or clues about their health would be leaked,' he wrote on X.

Similar reports have emerged about Xi's fellow dictator and 'good friend' Vladimir Putin.

Officials travelling with the Russian president on international visits reportedly collect his excrement in special bags, which are kept in a dedicated briefcase.

The Xi rumours matter because he has turned himself into China's most powerful leader since Mao Zedong, ruthlessly removing opponents and abolishing time limits on his rule – effectively making himself leader for life.

A purge at the top of the military has removed 36 generals and lieutenants (with another 65 missing or potentially purged) since 2022, according to an analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

They included earlier this summer Zhang Youxia, who was second in command of the military under Xi, and who was accused of disloyalty, corruption and other serious disciplinary breaches.

There is no obvious successor to Xi and he has avoided anointing one, fearing that person might become a threat.

It is fair to assume that he has made a lot of enemies, which increases the likelihood of a possibly violent power struggle to take over from him.

This is precisely what Deng Xiaoping sought to avoid.

It was Deng – who led China after a power struggle following the death of Mao – who introduced

a ten–year time–limit on leaders' tenure in office and a more collective form of leadership to ensure a smoother transition between premiers, safeguards now swept away by Xi.

For all his country's modernity – not least its cutting–edge technology and economic achievements – Xi has taken its politics back to the days of dynastic China. He has surrounded himself with sycophants, and loyalty to Xi is now the single most important requirement of those in positions of power.

His health is a closely guarded state secret, amplifying the speculation each time there are signs that he is flagging.

'In a system where so much power is monopolised by one man, the physical condition of that man is no longer merely a personal matter – it becomes a matter of consequence for the entire country,' according to Shum.

His book, Red Roulette: An Insider's Story Of Wealth, Power, Corruption And Vengeance In Today's China, lifts the lid on the country's systemic corruption. 

And the impact of Xi's health could be far worse than Shum suggests, since it could ripple well beyond China's borders as rivals manoeuvre for position, each attempting to sound stronger and more jingoistic on issues ranging from Taiwan to global competition with the US.

What China does or doesn't do is now far more consequential for the world than it was in Mao's day, and the prospect of Beijing consumed by a struggle for power will alarm Western leaders. China was isolated under Mao. Now it is responsible for a third of the world's manufacturing output. Fallout from either political paralysis or violent upheaval would shake the world economy.

Xi became party leader in 2012 after a power struggle with a popular provincial party boss and amid coup rumours involving the then head of state security. Judging by his military purges, Xi still worries about the loyalty of the army – the world's largest.

The threat of violence – even civil war – haunts a party with a turbulent history and which no longer has a mechanism for orderly transferring power. Taiwan might become collateral damage, as an ailing Xi seeks to fulfil his pledge to grab the island – or hardline rivals embrace the jingoistic slogans of 're–unification'.

The rapid deterioration of Mao's physical and mental health towards the end of his life showed the lengths the CCP will go to maintain the secrecy surrounding the health of its leaders.

His descent into decrepitude was subject to a massive cover–up. Even the CIA was fooled. A secret report in 1975 concluded: 'There is no evidence the chairman is especially troubled by health problems.'

A year after that report, Mao suffered his third heart attack and died four days later.

He also had Parkinson's disease and, according to a memoir by his personal doctor, spent his final years in a state of clinical paranoia. His death unleashed a vicious power struggle before Deng emerged as paramount leader.

The case of Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev, who ruled the USSR from 1964 until his death in 1982, provides another uncomfortable warning about the impact of secrecy, lies and paranoia about a leader's health.

In his final years he could barely function. During a 1979 summit in Vienna with US President Jimmy Carter, he struggled to pay attention and his speech was slurred. He picked his way through a banquet using only a small spoon, while his spokesman insisted he was in 'excellent health'.

Brezhnev's decline was accompanied by economic stagnation as the Soviet Union ran out of ideas. The hopeless state of the country seemed to match that of its geriatric leader.

It did generate one boom though – in jokes that eroded the legitimacy of the party and the gerontocracy that ran it, turning it into a laughing stock. 'Did you go to the latest funeral?' asked one joke. 'Yes, I've got a season ticket,' came the reply.

Another asked the difference between a crocodile and the party's central committee.

'A crocodile has 40 teeth and four legs,' came the reply, 'while the central committee has four teeth and 40 legs.'

Xi Jinping is not Leonid Brezhnev – at least not yet.

And in the days of social media, it is far more difficult to hide the physical ailments of leaders. The old jokes have been replaced by internet memes.

And as hard as the CCP tries to control the internet, the trials of Winnie–the–Pooh will inevitably slip through the cracks.

There is often a fine line between tyranny and absurdity. No more so than when the party is seeking to cover up or deny the blindingly obvious at the behest of an all–powerful leader, which can quickly eat away at its legitimacy.

It seems no coincidence that days after Xi returned from the Washington summit, as speculation grew about possible illness, state media pictured him chairing what was described as a 'national meeting on health' – not his, but the nation's.

'Xi calls for decisive progress in Healthy China advancement,' trumpeted the Xinhua state news agency, in an almost cartoonish attempt to give Xi as much authority as it could muster on the issue of healthy living.

In the looking–glass world of the CCP, that is perhaps as clear a sign as you will find that all is not well.

- Ian Williams is author of Vampire State: The Rise And Fall Of The Chinese Economy.
news.summary: The demand for the room was highly unusual, according to US officials, and may hold the secret of a gathering mystery - that of the true state of the Chinese leader's health.

news.title: Ilhaan Cumar waxay qorsheyneysaa inay ka guurto gurigeeda Washington
news.text:
Okt 25 (Jowhar)- Xildhibaanad Ilhaan Cumar oo ka tirsan Aqalka Kongareeska Mareykanka ayaa sheegtay inay ka guuri doonto gurigeeda Washington, DC, iyadoo ku sababeysay walaac dhanka amniga ah ka dib markii dhawaan ay weerar ku qaadeen hantida wakiillada federaalka Mareykanka.

Wareysi ay siisay MS NOW Arbacadii, Cumar ayaa markii ugu horreysay ka hadashay weerarka, iyadoo xustay in dhacdadu ay ka dhigtay inay dareento ammaan darro halkaas.

Toddobaadkii hore, saraakiishu waxay baadheen guriga Cumar iyadoo la adeegsanayo waxa afhayeenka Waaxda Caddaaladda uu ku tilmaamay “waraaq baaritaan oo sharcigu ogol yahay”, isagoo intaa ku daray in weerarku uu qayb ka ahaa “baaritaan dambiyeed oo socda oo federaal ah”.

Sida laga soo xigtay NBC News, oo soo xiganaysa hal qof oo arrintan yaqaan, dacwadaha mustaqbalka ee laga yaabo in lagu soo oogo Ilhaan waxaa ka mid noqon kara shirqool iyo hadallo been abuur ah oo ku jira warqadaheeda socdaalka. Cumar waxay beenisay khaladka waxayna ku eedeysay maamulka cabsi gelin siyaasadeed.

Ilhaan, oo ku dhalatay Soomaaliya isla markaana ah muwaadin Mareykan ah oo dhalasho qaatay, ayaa sheegtay inay “ku kalsoon tahay xaqiiqda ah inaan wax qalad ah sameyn”.

Xildhibaanadda Dimuqraadiga ah ee Minnesota ee horumarsan ayaa si joogto ah u dhaleeceyn jirtay oo bartilmaameed u ahayd Madaxweynaha Mareykanka Donald Trump, kaasoo dhowr jeer ku riixay in la maxkamadeeyo cadawgiisa siyaasadeed ee la aaminsan yahay.

Horraantii toddobaadkan, Trump wuxuu haweeneyda aqalka Congress-ka ku tilmaamay “mid xanuunsan” oo “aan daacad ahayn” wuxuuna ku tilmaamay goobtii ay ku dhalatay inay tahay “guri dhab ah”.

Sannado badan, Cumar, oo Muslim ah, waxaa bartilmaameed u ahaa aragtiyo shirqool ah oo ka dhan ah xaaladda socdaalka, oo ay ku jiraan eedeymo sheegaya inay guursatay walaalkeed.

Haweeneyda aqalka Congress-ka ee Minnesota ayaa si isdaba joog ah u beenisay eedeymahaas iyagoo ku tilmaamay “been xun”.

news.title: 'Saddam Hussein Opened a Cheesecake Factory': Former President Barack Obama Mocks Trump's White House
news.text: Barack Obama mocked Donald Trump's White House renovations at a Saturday campaign rally in Ohio, declaring, 'He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.' The former president was campaigning for Democrats ahead of the autumn midterm elections.His visit to the near-capacity Public Auditorium supported Amy Acton, the Democratic nominee for governor, and former senator Sherrod Brown, who is seeking to regain his Senate seat. Polls placed both races as toss-ups in a state that has become more reliably Republican since Trump's political rise.Obama criticised the president's ballroom construction and gold accents at the White House, contrasting those projects with the issues facing voters.'Does anybody really think this guy in the White House right now is spending all that time thinking about these issues?' he questioned. 'I mean, I don't know if you've noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovations. He should be on HGTV.'Obama Mocks Trump's White House RenovationsThe Cheesecake Factory comparison drew amusement from the crowd inside the auditorium, which holds more than 10,000 people. Obama delivered several quips during his afternoon address, but much of his 35-minute speech focused on Trump's record and campaign promises.He urged voters to assess whether the president had delivered on promises to control costs. Obama argued that Trump's tariffs and the war in Iran had instead contributed to rising prices.'In this case, this administration's actions are directly responsible for rising costs,' Obama stated. 'The current president chose to make a series of bad decisions. Most importantly, he decided to start an unnecessary war that nobody asked for, nobody voted for.'Obama Challenges Ramaswamy Over Acton AdvertisementObama also criticised an attack advertisement aired by Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, featuring Acton's estranged mother, Donna Arthur, calling her daughter a 'liar'. NBC News reported bipartisan condemnation of the advertisement for drawing on a family's history of alleged sexual abuse.Acton has stated that she has not seen or spoken to Arthur in nearly 50 years. She has described being sexually abused as a child by Arthur's then-husband and stated that she was removed from Arthur's custody in 1978 after her then-stepfather was charged with rape.Obama stated, 'I don't know what's happened where the standards of behavior have gotten so low that somebody can run an ad like that.'At the rally, Acton accused her opponent of exploiting her childhood to rescue his campaign. Ramaswamy defended the advertisement, and his campaign told NBC News on Thursday that it planned a $4 million (£2.99 million) push to air it. Trump also expressed approval, according to the report.Obama Rally Draws Republican ResponsesRamaswamy spokesperson Connie Luck responded that Ohioans could not afford a liberal governor who attended events with Obama but failed to support them.Amy Natoce, a spokesperson for Senator Jon Husted, Brown's Republican rival, also criticised the Democrats' appearance together. 'The sight of Sherrod Brown and Barack Obama together again should send shivers down Ohioans' spines,' she stated. news.title: Five parties are campaigning on KiwiSaver changes. How would each affect you? – Brian Fallow
news.text:
But it would not impose compulsion on employees, preserving the agency and flexibility they have now. The employer’s contribution would continue to rise even if the employee pauses theirs. 

Both National and Labour would have the Government provide employer contributions during paid parental leave, and remove the current provision allowing employers to stop their contributions for workers over 65 who are still contributing to KiwiSaver. 

New Zealand First calls for compulsory membership, with contribution rates of 8 per cent for both employees and employers “initially” rising to 10% “eventually”. No timetable or other details are offered, apart from a plan to cut the corporate tax rate for SMEs – companies with revenue of less than $30 million a year – from 28% to 20%. That would offer some relief for what would be hefty increases in payroll costs. 

All we can conclude is that NZ First would probably not block National’s plan, and would be content to say it didn’t go far enough. 

Act proposes no changes to contributions, apart from the already legislated increase in the default rate to 4 per cent in 2028. It opposes compulsion. 

Instead, it would stop taxing the investment earnings of KiwiSaver funds, allowing compound interest to work its magic. Last year, those earnings topped $10 billion. We are one of only seven OECD countries to tax the investment income of retirement savings. 

Act reckons the fiscal cost would average about $1 billion a year over the next four years, but half of that would be clawed back by scrapping what remains of the Government contribution, which has been halved this year to a maximum of $5 a week. 

Clearly, this tax change would benefit those on higher incomes most. Eliminating the Government contribution would make it even more regressive. But KiwiSaver is not really designed to address horizontal income inequality. You have to look elsewhere in the tax system for that. 

The Opportunity Party’s “KiwiSaver 2.0” resembles National’s plan in being compulsory for both employees and employers and rising to a minimum of 6% for both. It would not allow withdrawals for first-home buyers, of which there were 50,000 last year. And it would phase in tax deductibility for contributions. 

It is part of Opportunity’s radical tax reset, which includes a land tax (atop the one already funding local government) and universal basic income. So nothing would happen for the next three years. The ratcheting up of contributions to 6% and the phasing in of deductibility would happen – if at all – over the six years after that. 

So how much money are we talking about? 

KiwiSaver’s regulator, the Financial Markets Authority, reports that, in the year to March, $13.2 billion was paid into KiwiSaver. That equates to 2.9 per cent of GDP. 

National’s plan would double that within the next six years. That’s while klaxons are blaring at Treasury and from much of the commentariat about projections that the fiscal cost of NZ Super might rise by 3 percentage points of GDP over the next 40 years. And that’s the gross cost; superannuitants pay tax. 

National proposes a similar increase compressed into just six years. How would the cost of ramping up KiwiSaver be split? Less take-home pay for employees, and therefore less consumer spending? Lower profit margins for employers, with less hiring and business investment? Or, to avoid those outcomes, higher prices for consumers – a wage/price spiral raising the risk of higher interest rates and more fiscal drag? So far, so unappealing. 

Then there’s the question, why go compulsory? Who would that affect? 

I remember a press conference 20 years ago when Michael Cullen was laying out how this new scheme of his would work. I asked him then if it was a Trojan horse for compulsion down the track. “Do I look like Brad Pitt?” was his reply. The movie Troy had come out the year before. So no. 

The main reason was that a compulsory deduction from people’s wages would feel like a new tax, even if, strictly speaking, it’s not, in that the money is not going to the Government. 

But that distinction would not cut much ice with the people being compelled to pay it. Especially for those at the lower end of the wage distribution, it would be an unwelcome innovation. If that was true then, it is even more so today, when foodbanks are reporting more and more people with jobs still struggling to put food on the table. 

So who is not paying into KiwiSaver, and why not? 

The Retirement Commission put out an illuminating report last year on the demographics of KiwiSaver. A key group is the 782,000 people aged between 18 and 64. They account for most of the just over 1 million KiwiSaver members who were not contributing, and they represent about a quarter of the total resident population in that age range. 

Nearly half of them had an annual income of less than $10,000. Another 35 per cent had incomes between $10,000 and $50,000, which is what a full year of 40-hour weeks at the minimum wage earns you. 

So we are talking about people working part-time, if at all, or for only part of the year. It’s not clear whether this is a rich vein of potential contribution income for KiwiSaver funds to mine. 

The other 15 per cent of that non-contributing age group, the commission says, includes self-employed people. For them, the employer contribution is irrelevant, and they might well prefer to keep that cash in their own businesses. 

Then there are the growing number of people 65 or over who continue in paid employment. On the current rules, which both National and Labour plan to change, they are not entitled to an employer contribution. 

So should Parliament look at these groups – the low-paid, the self-employed and working superannuitants – and say these people are feckless and improvident? If they won’t pay into KiwiSaver voluntarily, they must be compelled to? 

National’s answer to the obvious question about those who simply can’t afford to contribute is to say they can seek an exemption, but they will need to satisfy the conditions that already apply for KiwiSaver hardship withdrawals. 

They don’t make it easy. Typically, the form you need to fill in about your financial circumstances is extremely detailed, and needs to be backed with documentary evidence. Then you need to track down a justice of the peace, or lawyer or other worthy, to witness you solemnly sign a statutory declaration. 

The compliance costs of requiring perhaps hundreds of thousands of people to jump through those hoops, for an exemption of uncertain duration, would be horrendous. 

So it looks like compulsion would do far more harm than good. Michael Cullen got that right. 

The Treasury modelling that underpinned last month’s Prefu includes forecasts that the average wage after tax will rise to $1471 a week by fiscal 2031. That represents a compound annual growth rate of 2.6% from current levels. Lop off half a percentage point a year for rising KiwiSaver contributions under National’s plan and you are down to just over 2%. And that’s nominal. What are the chances inflation will average 2% a year for the next five years? 

It would certainly be a change from the past five years, when it averaged 4.3%, for well-known reasons: Covid, Ukraine, Donald Trump’s weaponisation of trade, and now the Gulf war. What are the odds that New Zealand will be sideswiped by similar shocks from the other 99.8% of the world over the next five years? 

If so, the growing exactions for KiwiSaver would come out of wages that, on average, after tax and inflation, are heading lower than even the current cost-of-living-crisis levels. 

Brian Fallow is a former economics editor of the NZ Herald.

news.summary: OPINION: It looks like compulsory KiwiSaver could do far more harm than good.

news.title: ‘A Disgrace’: Trump Reacts to Sledgehammer Attack on Iwo Jima Memorial
news.text:
President Donald Trump called the sledgehammer attack on an Iwo Jima statue near Marine Corps Base Quantico a “disgrace” after police arrested a man accused of knocking the head off one of the figures.

Trump made the remarks when a reporter asked what his message was to someone who disrespects a memorial honoring fallen Marines and what should happen to the person responsible.

“What he did to that beautiful memorial was terrible. I guess he comes from Mexico,” Trump said. “He came in through the border of Biden, the open border of Biden and we nabbed him.”

“But what he did to that beautiful memorial, very important memorial, was a disgrace,” he added.

Trump did not specify what punishment he believed the suspect should receive.

Prince William County police identified the suspect as Miguel Alonso Maldonado Soriano, 27, of Stafford, Virginia. Officers responded to a report of property destruction near Richmond Highway and Fuller Road in Quantico at approximately 10:13 p.m. Wednesday, October 21. Police said they arrived to find him striking the statue with a sledgehammer.

Officers detained Maldonado Soriano without incident. The damage included the removal of one figure’s head, along with other damage to the sculpture. Police estimated the losses at hundreds of thousands of dollars.

He faces charges of felony destruction of property, trespass with intent to damage property, and felony injury to a monument. The department’s October 22 report listed him as being held without bond, with a court date pending. The report did not identify a motive.

Maldonado Soriano entered the United States illegally in December 1999. He received Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals status under the Obama administration in 2014 and that protection was extended under the Biden administration in 2024. His DACA protection ended under the Trump administration this year.

President Donald Trump called the sledgehammer attack on an Iwo Jima statue near Marine Corps Base Quantico a “disgrace” after police arrested a man accused of knocking the head off one of the figures.

WASHINGTON, United States: Former US president Barack Obama delivered scathing criticisms of his successor, Donald Trump, at rallies Saturday in Ohio and Michigan to support Democratic candidates ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.

Democrats are attempting to wrest back control of one or both chambers of the US Congress, which are currently controlled by Trump’s Republican party.

“Imagine the power duo of Abdul and Elissa,” Obama said, referring to the incumbent Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin, who is not up for election this year.

“You got a Muslim man, you got a Jewish woman fighting for you in the United States Senate. That’s something, Michigan, you can be proud of.”

news.title: Kim Jong Un inaugurates China border bridge
news.text: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited China on Saturday, inaugurating a new bridge that connects the two countries and saying he hoped to expand cooperation with his powerful neighbour.Kim’s visit to China is his latest move in an increasingly assertive foreign policy as he seeks to align Pyongyang with Beijing and Moscow in a united front against the United States under what he portrays as a “new Cold War.” It’s his first visit in a year.Kim arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong Saturday after crossing the newly opened bridge, according to South Korea’s Unification Ministry, which handles affairs related to North Korea and China’s official Xinhua News Agency. He met with Wang Huning, a member of the Standing Committee of China’s Communist Party. The two toured a car factory and promised to strengthen the bilateral relationship.Kim said that his country “stands ready to work with China to carry forward their historical friendship and expand practical cooperation, thereby delivering tangible benefits to the peoples of both countries,” according to Xinhua. Wang then accompanied Kim to the bridge to send him off, according to Xinhua.Experts said the opening of the New Yalu River Bridge this month was a key symbol of strengthening ties between North Korea and China and reflected their intent to expand trade, as it is expected to accommodate two-way traffic around the clock, including container shipments and heavy cargo trucks. North Korean state media did not immediately report on Kim’s visit, and China’s Foreign Ministry press office did not respond to a request for confirmation.Citing anonymous diplomatic sources, Japan’s Kyodo News agency reported earlier on Saturday that Chinese authorities were imposing strict traffic restrictions in parts of Dandong and all hotel rooms in those areas were unavailable for reservation. Japan’s TBS television network aired footage of what it said was likely Kim’s motorcade in Dandong, including a black limousine bearing North Korean flags.Kim has recently sought to strengthen ties with China, the North’s traditional main ally and economic lifeline, after years of prioritising ties with Russia.He sent thousands of troops and conventional weapons to support President Vladimir Putin’s war in Ukraine, possibly in exchange for military and economic assistance.Kim’s visit is timed to a key battle anniversary in the Korean War with China--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------Kim’s latest visit to China is his sixth since taking power in late 2011 following the death of his father. The visit appears to be timed to underscore the strength of his ties with Beijing ahead of the Oct. 25 anniversary of China’s first major victory in the Korean War, which was days after Chinese troops crossed the Yalu River into North Korea in October 1950.The war began with North Korea’s surprise attack on the South in June 1950, prompting a UN-led coalition headed by the United States to intervene and push back the offensive. North Korea was backed primarily by Chinese forces, with assistance from the then-Soviet Union’s air force, before fighting ended with a 1953 armistice that left the peninsula technically at war.Kim said his visit on Saturday was also to memorialise the martyrs in the war, according to Xinhua.Chinese President Xi Jinping travelled to Pyongyang in June for a meeting with Kim. During their summit, Xi expressed Beijing’s willingness to expand bilateral cooperation in trade, agriculture, construction and technology, while Kim described ties with China as a top strategic priority.Kim last visited Beijing in September 2025, when he met with Xi and watched a military parade alongside Putin and other foreign leaders.Kim has maintained a hard line toward Seoul and has so far rebuffed a proposal from US President Donald Trump to revive their diplomacy, which broke down in 2019 during Trump’s first term. Kim’s government has called for Washington to abandon its “hostile policy” and drop demands for the North’s denuclearisation as a precondition for renewed talks.South Korea’s spy agency told lawmakers last month that it saw a 50% possibility of a meeting between Trump and Kim on the sidelines of next month’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, or APEC, summit in Shenzhen, China.

news.title: Ukraine, Russia consider renewed peace talks amid ongoing conflict
news.text: Ukraine and Russia have signalled their willingness to resume US-brokered peace talks and are backing a humanitarian mission led by First Lady Melania Trump. But deep disagreements over territory and security guarantees that re-emerged this week underscore obstacles to ending the war.The new diplomatic push comes after more than 4½ years of fighting, bringing with it a surprise announcement on Friday: Kyiv and Moscow have agreed to a local ceasefire to allow aid next week into a stranded town in Ukraine’s southern war-divided region of Kherson, following secret consultations between Melania Trump and civilian negotiators from Russia and Ukraine. While the initiative raised hopes of similar humanitarian missions in the future, there were few indications that any of the key positions have shifted.Russia continues to demand Ukrainian territory it does not fully control, while Kyiv insists any agreement must include ironclad guarantees against another invasion. Within hours of Russian President Vladimir Putin saying he agreed “in principle” to restart talks, Russia launched a deadly barrage of ballistic missiles and drones on Kyiv. Moscow on the same day said it had destroyed more than 800 Ukrainian drones heading toward its cities. Here’s a look at where the two countries stand as potential negotiations loom. US presidential envoy Steve Witkoff secured the latest commitment to talks after shuttling between Oslo, Norway, and St. Petersburg, Russia, this week to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Putin. A new round of negotiations would be the fourth brokered by the Trump administration, following the most recent round in Geneva in February.A Kremlin spokesman said that the next round of talks is likely to be held in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, around mid-November. Western governments backing the peace initiative are seeking a new formula to break the impasse while acknowledging that territorial and security questions remain unresolved.US President Donald Trump’s ties with Zelenskyy, meanwhile, have sunk to a new low. Moscow has been bolstered by Trump’s deal for Russia to supply the US with diesel and his recent rejection of new Russia sanctions. Kyiv has been undermined by disruptions in satellite support for its drones after rejecting a call by the US president to halt strikes on Russian oil infrastructure. Ukrainian leaders fear the moves will embolden Putin, giving him little incentive to compromise at the negotiating table.As Trump increased pressure on Zelenskyy, accusing him of being an obstacle to peace, Witkoff secured the release of an American who had been jailed for more than four years on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine. The envoy described the Russian leader as a “humanitarian” at their meeting in St Petersburg -- a remark met with consternation in Ukraine.The two sides are still far apart--------------------------------------While both sides back calls for new talks, Russia and Ukraine are still far apart on their terms for a settlement, while their armies remain locked on the battlefield and they pummel each other with daily long-range strikes.Central to Russia’s demands is full control of four Ukrainian regions it illegally annexed months after the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022: Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson, in addition to Crimea, which Moscow seized in 2014.Russia currently occupies about 20 per cent of Ukraine but has failed to capture all the territory in the regions over which it claims sovereignty.In a long list of demands, Moscow also wants Ukraine to withdraw forces from all four annexed regions, renounce its bid to join NATO, reduce the size of its military and drop restrictions against the Russian language and a Moscow-affiliated branch of the Orthodox Church.Speaking on state television late Thursday, Putin said Moscow remains “ready to negotiate and seek solutions to this difficult, complex situation,” before adding: “But if some prefer a different path, so be it. In any case, all the objectives of the special military operation will be achieved.”Zelenskyy -- who for months has publicly advocated for peace talks -- argues that giving up land would leave Ukraine more vulnerable to future attacks. Kyiv views security guarantees as essential to prevent Russia from restarting the war in the future.The Ukrainian president has reaffirmed support for a ceasefire that would freeze front-line positions, followed by talks on conditions for ending the war. Moscow has rejected a break in hostilities until a comprehensive agreement on its terms is reached.Security guarantees remain unresolved----------------------------------------------While Kyiv and Moscow have maintained limited contact to organise prisoner exchanges and the return of fallen soldiers, previous talks have made no progress on the security arrangements needed to sustain a peace deal.Ukraine believes security guarantees backed by Western allies are essential to any future settlement, ideally in the form of NATO membership -- an option Vladimir Putin has rejected. Ukraine expects to heavily rely on its own army as the main security guarantee with financial backing from its allies.Other elements of security guarantees being discussed range from NATO membership, which the US administration has currently ruled out, direct guarantees from the United States in what Zelenskyy has described as an “Article 5-like format,” and backing by the European-led 30-country alliance known as the Coalition of the Willing.Article 5 of the NATO charter contains the alliance’s mutual-defence guarantee, which establishes that an attack on one is an attack on all.“All of these guarantees are possible on the basis of a strong Ukrainian army -- in terms of both numbers and quality -- with clear funding, and not a small amount. Our colleagues in Europe and America know this,” Zelenskyy told reporters Thursday at a briefing.Following the massive attacks on Kyiv and other cities this week, he argued that only increased Western pressure on Moscow would change its calculations about future peace talks.“It is important to keep trying to find the right solutions to end this war,” Zelenskyy wrote in an online post. “But when Russia responds to negotiations with ballistic missiles, real pressure on Russia is needed to bring about different steps -- steps toward ending the killing.”
news.author: Derek Gatopoulos,Susie Blann

news.title: Trump eyes even more business with Russia after Ukraine war ends...as Moscow diesel tanker heads for US port
news.text:
President Donald Trump has signaled he is ready to expand America's business dealings with Russia once the war in Ukraine ends, just as a tanker carrying Russian diesel heads toward the US under his controversial agreement with Vladimir Putin.

The president declared on Saturday that Washington could resume commercial ties with Moscow after a peace agreement, despite mounting criticism over his decision to reopen American markets to Russian fuel while the Kremlin continues its invasion of Ukraine.

'Certainly, we'll do business with Ukraine and with Russia after this war ends, I would think,' Trump said.

The president added that he wanted to 'get back to life where Russia and Ukraine make a deal, and then we'd be able to do business with both.'

His comments came as the first shipment of Russian diesel under the new arrangement made its way across the Atlantic, with the vessel bound for New York and expected to arrive November 7.

The shipment marks a dramatic reversal in Washington's approach to Moscow and has sparked outrage in Kyiv, where Ukrainian officials fear the agreement could provide Putin with fresh funds to sustain his war.

Asked on Saturday about Russian interest in investing in Alaska's natural gas industry, Trump declined to address the proposal directly but made clear he envisioned a future in which American companies could again conduct business with Russia.

Trump also touted his administration's natural resources agreement with Ukraine, suggesting the arrangement could eventually be worth as much as $1 trillion.

He argued that the United States should have demanded greater financial compensation for the billions of dollars in assistance provided to Kyiv under former President Joe Biden.

'I feel foolish because all you had to do is ask them, and they would have paid. Meaning the European Union would have paid,' Trump said.

His remarks came just one day after the Kremlin announced that the first Russian diesel shipment under Trump's agreement with Putin was already underway.

'The first oil tanker has sailed off to customers, and regular supplies will continue,' Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov declared Friday.

Marine intelligence company Kpler reported that the vessel was heading for New York as its destination, with an estimated arrival date of November 7.

When completed, the delivery will be the first shipment of Russian diesel to the United States since July 2023.

Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said the initial cargo would contain approximately 40,000 tons of diesel, equivalent to roughly 300,000 barrels.

Trump has suggested the agreement could eventually bring millions more tons of Russian fuel into the United States as his administration battles stubbornly high energy prices ahead of the midterm elections.

But energy experts have questioned whether the imports will provide any meaningful relief to American consumers.

The inaugural shipment represents just 7% of the roughly 4million barrels of diesel consumed across the US every day.

The deal has drawn criticism from Republicans and Democrats alike over its legality and the prospect of strengthening Russia's finances during the ongoing conflict.

For Ukraine, the agreement represents another bitter setback in its efforts to isolate Putin economically and pressure Moscow into ending the invasion launched in February 2022.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky delivered a stinging rebuke of the arrangement, describing it as 'a weak decision by strong partners.'

The agreement is particularly contentious because it follows Trump's decision to approve sweeping sanctions targeting countries that continue to purchase Russian energy.

That package called for tariffs of up to 100 percent against the five largest importers of Russian oil or natural gas, although Trump suspended implementation of the measures before striking his new diesel arrangement with Putin.

The apparent policy U-turn comes as Russia's own fuel industry faces continuing pressure from Ukrainian drone attacks on its refineries.

Those strikes previously contributed to shortages inside Russia, although the disruption has since eased.

Last month Trump urged Kyiv to halt the refinery attacks, adding another source of friction to his increasingly strained relationship with Zelensky.

Despite the tensions, diplomatic efforts to end the fighting remain underway.

Zelensky revealed on Friday that he had spoken with Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner following their consultations with Putin in St. Petersburg.

The envoys had also held discussions with the Ukrainian leader earlier in the week in Norway.

A potential three-way meeting involving Washington, Moscow and Kyiv could take place next month, although no venue has been announced.

'We need diplomacy to move forward,' Zelensky told Washington's Hudson Institute.

The Ukrainian president warned that his country urgently needs additional American-made Patriot missile interceptors, financial assistance and protection for its power infrastructure as winter approaches.

He also complained that restrictions affecting Starlink and Starshield satellite services were hampering Ukrainian drone operations.
news.summary: Donald Trump has signaled plans to expand US business ties with Russia once the Ukraine war ends, despite mounting criticism of his controversial fuel deal with Vladimir Putin.

news.title: Brazil's Lula, Bolsonaro close arguments to voters ahead of nail-biting election runoff
news.text:
SAO PAULO -- Final arguments to voters in Brazil's presidential election were made Saturday, the eve of the runoff between incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro. Tens of thousands of supporters took to the streets hoping to lure the few undecided voters left.

Polls published on Saturday suggest it will be a nail-biting election that could be decided on details.

A victory for Bolsonaro would add Brazil to a list of Latin American countries — including Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica and Peru — that have elected allies of U.S. President Donald Trump in recent years. A win for Lula secures some distance between the region’s economic powerhouse and Washington.

The 80-year-old Lula, who lost the first round to the 45-year-old Bolsonaro by more than 2.2 million votes, possibly had the biggest rally of his career on Sao Paulo's key artery, Paulista Avenue. 

Bolsonaro brought supporters out in his native Rio de Janeiro and in Belo Horizonte, the capital of Minas Gerais, the state which for decades has correctly pointed to the winner of the country's election.

Saturday's demonstrations marked the culmination of a push that intensified earlier this month. 

Lula, who had a rally in Rio's Copacabana beach in the morning, told supporters "the people have taken it upon themselves to lead the campaign.” 

Since the Oct. 4 vote, massive leftist demonstrations have taken place in Brazil, a territory that supporters of the president had lost in recent years to voters of former President Jair Bolsonaro.

Almost 160 million Brazilians are eligible to vote. More than 33 million, or 21% of the electorate, did not vote earlier this month, and could face a small fine for failing to cast a ballot without justification. People who missed the first round can vote in the second.

Brazilians cast ballots using electronic voting machines, punching in digits that correspond to their candidates. Results are reported within hours after polls close.

Follow AP’s coverage of Latin America and the Caribbean at https://apnews.com/hub/latin-america
news.summary: The last arguments to voters in Brazil’s presidential election are being made on the eve of the runoff between incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro
news.author: Mauricio Savarese Associated Press

news.title: Attorney General Defends Alaska Election Lawsuit as Murkowski Pushes Back
news.text: Attorney General Todd Blanche defended the Justice Department’s lawsuit over Alaska’s closely watched Senate election on Saturday, as Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski said the department “should never have filed” the case. The unusual legal battle centers on two Senate candidates who share the same first and last names: incumbent Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan and retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. The dispute comes in a race that could help determine control of the Senate. Blanche said in a post on X that the Justice Department “does not seek to stop any ballot from being cast or to stop the certification of Alaska’s election.” “This litigation seeks to ensure that after Alaskans cast their ballots, they are preserved in a manner so that only Alaska’s governing officials have the information necessary to make a determination as to whether Alaskan voters were confused or mislead [sic],” Blanche wrote. He added: “The lawsuit was written by Justice Department attorneys and the Department did not coordinate with any campaign or candidate, but rather relied solely on federal law.” The statement comes after President Donald Trump said Friday that he had told the DOJ to bring the lawsuit. Trump has endorsed the incumbent Sullivan and repeatedly alleged that Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.’s candidacy was intended to confuse voters and hurt the senator. At a rally in Florida on Friday, Trump called the situation “cheating like hell.” Newsweek reached out to Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign, Senator Sullivan’s campaign, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. and the Alaska Division of Elections for comment on Saturday. Lisa Murkowski Says DOJ ‘Should Never Have Filed’ Alaska Lawsuit Murkowski, an Alaska Republican who has frequently broken with Trump, pushed back against the Justice Department’s case on Saturday. “Alaskans don’t need any help voting for their preferred candidates, and the State of Alaska has already handled this by clearly distinguishing the candidates on this year’s ballot,” Murkowski wrote on X. “The Department of Justice should never have filed this lawsuit.” On the ballot, the incumbent appears as Dan S. Sullivan and is labeled “Incumbent,” while the other candidate is listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. Alaska election officials removed Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. from the ballot after concluding his candidacy was intended to confuse or mislead voters, but he challenged the decision and was later restored to the ballot by the courts. Why Is the DOJ Suing Alaska Over the Senate Election? The Justice Department filed its lawsuit Thursday against Alaska and state election officials, alleging that Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.’s candidacy was intended to mislead voters into backing him instead of the incumbent. The DOJ contends the “sole purpose” of his candidacy is to benefit Peltola by reducing the number of votes cast for Senator Sullivan. The DOJ is seeking to block certification if Senator Sullivan loses by fewer votes than Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. receives, pending an investigation into potential voter confusion. Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. has rejected the suggestion that his candidacy is illegitimate. After he was restored to the ballot earlier this year, he said he was running because he was dissatisfied with the incumbent’s representation. “It’s a free country,” he said at the time, according to Courthouse News Service. “Most Alaskans are proud Independents and it’s my sincere hope that people know who and what they are voting for but ultimately, choice is good and voters’ intent will be as varied as the candidates who are running.” Trump Says He Told DOJ to Bring Alaska Lawsuit In a Truth Social post Wednesday, Trump called Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.’s candidacy a “SCAM” and said his administration was looking at “powerful legal options” to remove him from the ballot. After the DOJ filed the case, Trump took credit for the move. “I’m the one that said ‘do it,’” he told reporters Friday. A motion seeking dismissal of the lawsuit has since cited Trump’s remark in arguing that the DOJ case was “filed at the behest” of the president. The motion, filed on behalf of two Alaska voters, the League of Women Voters of Alaska and Common Cause, also asks the court to consider sanctions against the Justice Department attorneys who signed the complaint. Election-law experts have also questioned the legal basis for the case. “The DOJ’s lawsuit is completely meritless,” Michael Morley, the Sheila M. McDevitt Professor of Law and faculty director of the Election Law Center at Florida State University, previously told Newsweek. Mark Brown, a professor at Capital University Law School, similarly previously told Newsweek that “no federal statute authorizes the relief the DOJ seeks” and called the lawsuit “frivolous.” Why the Alaska Senate Race Matters The dispute comes just days before the November 3 midterm elections, with the Alaska contest among the races that could determine control of the U.S. Senate. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority. Peltola is seeking to become the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Alaska since Mark Begich won in 2008. Alaska uses ranked-choice voting. If no candidate wins more than 50 percent of first-choice votes, the lowest-performing candidate is eliminated and those ballots are redistributed according to voters’ subsequent choices until one candidate has a majority. Four candidates are competing in the Senate race: Peltola, Senator Dan S. Sullivan, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. and Gerald Heikes.
news.summary: Todd Blanche defends the DOJ’s Alaska election lawsuit as Lisa Murkowski says the department should never have filed it.
news.author: Steve Mollman

news.title: Obama Goes Scorched Earth on Trump at Packed Ohio Rally
news.text:
Barack Obama unleashed a blistering attack on President Donald Trump and the “not serious” people running the country, mocking the president’s White House renovations and accusing him of using the Oval Office to enrich himself and his family.

Speaking at his first midterm campaign rally Saturday, the former president joked that Trump had made the White House look “like Saddam Hussein opened up a Cheesecake Factory.”

Portraying Trump as an agent of “chaos and cruelty” and a man of broken promises, Obama told the crowd: “You remember that old thing about ‘drain the swamp’?”

“The only thing that got drained was the Reflecting Pool in the National Mall after some no-bid contract got it all messed up,” he said as the crowd erupted in laughter.

Obama delivered the remarks Saturday at a rally in support of Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton, a former top health director who was the target of a vicious MAGA attack ad, and former Sen. Sherrod Brown, who is trying to unseat GOP incumbent, former college football player, and object of Trump’s affection Jon Husted.

Crowds lined up for hours, with lines stretching around several downtown blocks, to get into Public Auditorium, which can accommodate up to 10,000 people.

The former president also took aim at Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s fixation on masculinity, mocking his emphasis on jawlines and testosterone levels and his desire to livestream executions.

“How much time does the defense secretary spend looking at himself in the mirror?” Obama asked, mocking Hegseth’s carefully styled hair. 

“These are not serious people!” 

Pointing to Trump’s broken promises on foreign wars and grocery prices, Obama asked: “Does anybody really think this guy in the White House right now is spending all that time thinking about these issues?

“I mean, I don’t know if you’ve noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovations,” he added. “He should be on HGTV.”

The remarks amounted to a withering critique of an administration Obama portrayed as more interested in macho posturing, vanity projects, and self-promotion than the business of governing.

But Obama also struck a more serious note, questioning what happened to decency in politics and arguing that the country cannot solve its problems without first repairing its moral compass.

With just days left in the campaign, Obama and Trump fanned out across battleground states Saturday, deploying their star power as the race for control of Congress entered its final stretch.

After Ohio, Obama headed to Detroit to support Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive Muslim doctor whose positions on Israel have alienated some Jewish voters and who has also struggled to win support among Black voters in Michigan.

Trump, meanwhile, was rallying Republicans in Georgia, where the party is fighting to hold a Senate seat and win the governor’s mansion. 

Obama’s appearance came days after Acton was targeted this week in a vile attack ad from her MAGA opponent in the governor’s race, Vivek Ramaswamy. 

“You probably heard by now, as a young child, my brother and I experienced a lot of child abuse and neglect,” Acton told the crowd. 

“We moved countless times as kids, and even wound up living in a tent in the middle of winter. And now my opponent has chosen to intentionally exploit my childhood to save his struggling campaign, but it’s not going to work.”

As the crowds started building before Obama’s speech, one attendee, Patricia Kellner, sported a white coat and a “Doctors for Dr Amy Acton” t-shirt as she held up a sign that said, “Fighting for Ohio.”

“I hope she wins,” she told the Daily Beast, “but you never know with all their dirty tricks.”

The ad featured Acton’s estranged mother calling her a liar. What it failed to explain was that the two have not spoken in decades after Acton’s mother sided with her stepfather, who had raped Acton as a child.

Trump backed the ad, which ignited a nationwide firestorm, with numerous Republicans urging Ramaswamy to take it down.

“We’re seeing independents break strongly for the Democrats,” one furious GOP strategist in Ohio told the Daily Beast. “I’m looking at early turnout results, and they’re up everywhere in the state.” 

Obama tore into Ramaswamy over the ad, accusing him of having no line he wouldn’t cross for the spotlight.

The MAGA candidate, however, spent Friday doubling down on the ad, claiming it had nothing to do with the sexual abuse his opponent suffered as a child.

“Our ad was about a consistent track record of Amy Acton telling lies, including during this campaign, and I do think that there has been very little to no coverage of the lies she has told about me, about my family, about my mother, and an ad they put up falsely calling me a murderer of a man’s wife.”

On Saturday, however, his campaign released a shorter version of the ad, removing a reference that challenged Acton’s account of growing up homeless and living in a tent.
news.summary:
Jeff Swensen / Getty ImagesBarack Obama unleashed a blistering attack on President Donald Trump and the “not serious” people running the country, mocking the president’s White House renovations and accusing him of using the Oval Office to enrich himself and his family.

Speaking at his first midterm campaign rally Saturday, the former president joked that Trump had made the White House look “like Saddam Hussein opened up a Cheesecake Factory.”

Read more at The Daily Beast.
news.author: Farrah Tomazin

news.title: Obama Mocks Trump's White House Renovations
news.text: Former President Barack Obama took several shots at President Donald Trump's focus on White House renovations during a rally in Ohio on Saturday, joking that Trump "should be on HGTV" and ridiculing reports of proposed changes, including a new ballroom, a revamped Rose Garden and additional gold décor. Obama quipped that Trump had the White House looking "like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory," drawing laughter from the audience. "What's up with the gold?" Obama joked. "There's gold everywhere." Newsweek has reached out to the White House via email on Saturday night for comment. Obama's remarks were notable because the former president has often avoided engaging directly with Trump in personal terms, preferring to focus on policy differences and broader concerns about American democracy. His remarks about the White House renovations represented an unusually direct jab at Trump. The gold accents match the finishes in Trump's residences and properties, including New York's Trump Tower and his Mar-a-Lago club in Florida. Obama told the Democratic crowd at the rally that it seemed unlikely Trump had spent much time thinking about lowering the cost of living and gas prices, given all the focus he has placed on renovations. During Trump's second term, the White House has also unveiled plans for a privately funded ballroom project on the South Lawn, while changes to landscaping around the Rose Garden have drawn criticism from some preservationists and praise from supporters who say the work modernizes the executive mansion. Obama mocked Trump's renovations by saying he had "paved over the Rose Garden" and was constructing a ballroom "bigger than the White House." At both of his appearances Saturday, including later Saturday in Michigan, Obama sharply criticized what he described as Trump’s corrupt leadership and accused Republican leaders of failing to hold the president accountable. "The only thing they drained was the reflecting pool," Obama said. Obama called this November 3 election the last chance to bring accountability to government for Trump's final two years in office. The crowd chanted "vote, vote, vote" in response. This is a breaking news article. Updates to follow.
news.summary: Former President Barack Obama mocked Donald Trump for focusing on White House construction projects, rather than domestic policy.
news.author: Jennifer Radcliffe

news.title: Brazil’s Lula, Bolsonaro draw thousands to election-eve rallies  | Barbados Gazette – Barbados &
news.text:
Brazil’s presidential candidates Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Flavio Bolsonaro have rallied thousands of supporters in a final show of campaign strength in advance of the country’s closely contested run-off election.

Donning a red hat, Lula addressed hundreds of supporters at Rio de Janeiro’s Copacabana Beach on Saturday, waving a Brazilian flag from a campaign truck as crowds gathered on the final day of campaigning.

“The people must choose either someone who kisses the national flag or someone who kisses the American flag”, the 80-year-old told the crowd as he referenced his opponent’s ties to US President Donald Trump.

Lula is seeking a fourth, non-consecutive term in Sunday’s run-off, which will task Brazilians with determining whether to stick with their incumbent left-wing leader or join a broader regional shift towards the right.

Bolsonaro, a senator and son of former far-right President Jair Bolsonaro, secured 47 percent of the vote in the first round, narrowly ahead of Lula’s 45 percent.

Recent polling shows Lula and the younger Bolsonaro remain about even on the eve of the pivotal election.

A CNT/MDA survey released on Saturday revealed Bolsonaro would receive 46.3 percent of the vote compared ⁠with 45 percent for the left-wing ⁠Lula. Last week, ⁠the poll showed a slightly closer race with Bolsonaro leading ⁠Lula 46.8 percent to ⁠45.9 percent.

The poll’s margin of error was 2.2 ‌percentage ‌points.

On Saturday, Bolsonaro’s supporters, including hundreds of motorcyclists wearing Brazil’s yellow national football shirts, gathered in the southeastern state of Minas Gerais.

One of those supporters, Ebert Dorigo, accused Lula’s Workers’ Party (PT) of encouraging dependence on government welfare, arguing a change in direction was needed for the country.

“The values we uphold are nation and family. Our country is divided today because, due to welfare-based policies, some people … haven’t grasped that improvement and achievement come only through hard work,” he told the news agency AFP.

The bitter campaign has exposed deep divisions over economic policy, crime and Brazil’s political future, which Bolsonaro has pledged to tackle with hundreds of thousands of more spots in prison and cuts to government spending.

His father, who served as president from 2019 to 2022, is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting a coup after losing that year’s election to Lula.

The two candidates struck a calmer tone during their final debate on Friday, although they traded accusations over the country’s economic difficulties and their respective records.

For some voters, however, the choice has been a difficult one.

“If there were any other candidate, that would be a better option,” Gabriela Ribeiro Viana, an event organiser, told AFP. “But we’re stuck choosing between the worst, the horrible, and the lesser evil”.

news.title: Israelis hold final rally against Netanyahu ahead of what may be the most consequential election in the country’s history
news.text:
Meanwhile, the death toll rose from Friday’s attack on a church in Jordan. And an Iranian military commander said his country will not allow U.S. warships to enter the Persian Gulf as concerns grow of a return to all-out war.

Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Saturday. Read our full coverage here.

Thousands rally in Tel Aviv days ahead of Israel’s election

A large crowd gathered in a final protest against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his government ahead of Tuesday’s close election.

The crowd heard calls for a commission of inquiry into the security failures that led to the Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023, that sparked the war in Gaza. Netanyahu has refused such an inquiry.

Netanyahu’s chief rival, Gadi Eisenkot, attended the rally that was an echo of the weekly ones once held to call for the release of hostages taken into Gaza. All hostages or their remains were eventually released, but Netanyahu has been accused of delaying deals to free them sooner.

Trump weighs more strikes or a deal with Iran

U.S. President Donald Trump bristled when asked how far he was from a possible attack on Iran. He recently said on social media he would not hit Iran again before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

“Do you really think I’m going to tell you if I’m going to do it?” Trump responded. “And there’s a possibility I will. There’s also a possibility we’ll have a nice, big, beautiful agreement.”

Trump repeated his assertion that Iran wants to make a deal, “but the problem is, will they hold the deal?”

Iran’s president accuses the US of disrupting negotiations

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian accused Washington of disrupting negotiations to end the war but said he still believes “we have to go and finish it.”

In comments aired on state television, he said Iran’s supreme leader had instructed Iranian officials to “go and finish it (the deal),” but “these scoundrels broke the rules of the game. We were holding talks, and they disrupted them.”

Anxiety has been growing in Iran and elsewhere that the U.S. or Israel will resume attacks before or just after Tuesday’s elections in Israel or the U.S. midterm elections.

Israel carries out arrests across Hebron after attack

Israeli forces carried out arrests and demolitions in Hebron in the occupied West Bank a day after two Palestinian gunmen killed two soldiers and wounded three others.

Up to 300 families left Deir Baha and two adjacent neighborhoods, according to a tally from Hebron’s municipality. Israel’s army didn’t respond to questions about the operation. On Friday, it said its forces had begun “conducting precise, targeted and thorough searches” in the area from where the gunmen operated.

Death toll from church attack in Jordan rises to 9

An ninth person died after gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in Jordan, state television reported. More than two dozen people were receiving treatment in hospitals.

Gunmen on Friday opened fire at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak, south of Jordan’s capital, Amman. Karak is home to a minority Christian population.

Airstrikes kill 15 people in Yemen, including a child

Strikes killed 11 people, including four children, in the Yemeni capital of Sanaa, according to the Health Ministry run by Iran-backed Houthi rebels. And an airstrike hit homes in Hodeida province, killing at least four people, health authorities said.

The Houthis blamed neighboring Saudi Arabia, which backs forces fighting the rebels. Saudi Arabia did not respond to a request for comment. The Associated Press couldn’t independently verify the claims.

At least two explosions were later heard near the international airport in Yemen’s southern city of Aden, the seat of the internationally recognized government. The Houthi military spokesperson said a military camp and a naval base were targeted. The government’s interior ministry said the Houthis attacked the coast guard headquarters at its complex with two ballistic missiles.

The Saudi-led coalition earlier said it intercepted three ballistic missiles fired by the Houthis toward the Saudi capital, Riyadh, and Taif and Yanbu cities.

The UAE closes beaches after oil spill from tanker

The United Arab Emirates closed beaches after an oil spill from a tanker. The spill impacted beaches of Umm Al Quwain, one of the seven emirates making up the federation, and cleanup efforts were underway, the Climate Change and Environment Ministry said.

The ministry said the spill poses no health risks but did not provide details about its scale. It came two weeks after Iran’s state-run broadcaster reported an oil tanker had struck a naval mine and caught fire while attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz without coordinating with Tehran.

Iran says it will not allow US warships to enter Persian Gulf

An Iranian military commander said Iran will not allow U.S. warships to enter the Persian Gulf or approach Iran’s territorial waters, according to the state-run IRNA news agency.

Gen. Ali Abdollahi, chief of staff of Iran’s armed forces and commander of its joint military command, also warned Trump that U.S. forces would never return to the Strait of Hormuz.

US reissues Mideast travel warnings over Houthi threats

The State Department reissued travel advisories for Americans in or traveling to the Middle East, citing threats posed by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels.

Bahrain, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates are covered by the warnings and have appeared in previous travel alerts since the start of the Iran war.

The department has reduced staffing at four U.S. embassies in the Middle East after receiving intelligence that Iran has stepped-up efforts to target American personnel.

news.title: Donald Trump casts midterm ballot early in Florida
news.text:
Mr Trump has been criticised in the past for voting by mail despite his long history of railing against that method of submitting ballots.

The midterm elections are on November 3.

Asked if he voted the party line, Mr Trump, who was wearing an “I Voted” sticker, said: “Very much so.”

Speaking to reporters at the poll site, the president again defended an ad from Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy.

The ad has faced intense blowback for featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Dr Amy Acton, who lost custody of her children after her husband, the children’s stepfather, was indicted for raping Ms Acton when she was 12.

Mr Trump also defended his decision to instruct his administration to file its lawsuit to block certification of the US Senate race in Alaska if Republican Senator Dan Sullivan loses over the inclusion of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot.

As for the war in Iran, he said: “I may have to finish it off. Or maybe they’ll make a deal, but I’m not sure. Either way, we win.”

Melania Trump, who this week brokered a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the ravaged, Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky so that humanitarian aid could be delivered and civilians evacuated, was asked whether she might travel to Ukraine.

“We will see,” she told reporters.

news.title: Trump prepares for Iran escalation after U.S. and Israeli elections
news.text: A Middle East war that U.S. President Donald Trump said would be over in a matter of weeks now looks set to escalate as it enters its eighth month.Trump has repeatedly hinted that his forces in the Mideast would resume strikes on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3. The president has already sent a third aircraft carrier strike group and 10,000 additional sailors and Marines toward the Persian Gulf to give U.S. commanders more options if he restarts hostilities. Last week, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth also made an unannounced stop in Israel — which launched the war against Iran alongside the U.S. — where he met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu just days ahead of the Israeli leader’s sensitive reelection bid. Staffing at Mideast bases, which have been hit hard by Iranian counterstrikes, has reportedly been reduced.
